zones.name: A vessel with no flag on the high seas
zones.essay:
Suppose a boat or a floating home goes out onto the open ocean and flies no country's flag, or flies one its owners designed themselves. This idea combines two things, the high seas, which no country owns, and a refusal of the registration that every ordinary ship carries. People who try it often reason that with no flag there is no law. The real position is narrower than that, and one part of it is still argued over.

Start with what is clearly settled. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Under Article 92 a ship on the high seas normally answers only to the country whose flag it flies, so a foreign warship may not simply come aboard. Article 110 lists the exceptions, and one is reasonable ground for suspecting that "the ship is without nationality". The warship may then send a boat under an officer to check the papers. If suspicion remains it may search further, and if the suspicion proves unfounded the ship must be compensated. This is called the right of visit. A ship that uses two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having none (Article 92(2)). Nobody seriously disputes the boarding power, so an unflagged vessel has no treaty protection from a stop and search. Calling this a gap in the law would be wrong, because Article 110 addresses it by name.

Older rulings say more. In 1946 a British destroyer stopped the Asya about 100 miles off Jaffa. She raised a Turkish flag, then hauled it down and raised a Zionist flag, which belonged to no state. In Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine (1948) the Privy Council, then the top court for the British Empire, said freedom of the open sea belongs to ships that fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a state, and that the Asya "could not claim the protection of any State". In United States v. Marino-Garcia (1982) a US appeals court upheld drug convictions of nine foreign crewmen on the Four Roses, stopped about 65 miles off Cuba with nothing linking the cargo to the United States. The court called stateless vessels "international pariahs" and required no connection to the United States.

The open question is what may follow the boarding. Article 110 speaks only of verifying and examining. By contrast, Article 105 lets any state seize a pirate ship and try those aboard, and Article 109 allows arrest for illegal broadcasting. No such words appear for a ship without nationality. So writers divide. The "any state" view holds that any country may apply its law to a stateless vessel, and Churchill and Lowe are cited for a broad power to intervene. The "nexus" view requires some link, such as the crew's nationality, and Bennett is cited for limiting a boarding state to inspection. In 2025 Andrew Norris argued that states have been needlessly timid and may assert full jurisdiction. In 2026 Thea Coventry of Leiden argued that boarding does not by itself give power over foreigners' conduct, and that "sailing a vessel without nationality is not itself an international crime". The Enrica Lexie tribunal accepted that states may exceptionally use high-seas freedoms through small non-registered vessels, which shows that being unregistered does not in every case mean being outside the law's protection. No international court has decided the point.

National courts have mostly gone one way, under their own statutes. The United States defines a "vessel without nationality" in the Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act (46 USC 70502), including a vessel whose named country denies the registry. In 2008 the Drug Trafficking Vessel Interdiction Act (18 USC 2285) made it a crime to operate an unflagged submersible beyond a territorial sea with intent to evade detection. In United States v. Aybar-Ulloa in 2021 the First Circuit, a US appeals court, held that international law permits prosecuting foreigners seized on a stateless vessel. A panel of the same court ruled in 2022 that one part of the definition went beyond what Congress could do, and the full court in 2023 cancelled that ruling on narrower grounds without deciding the question. The Eleventh Circuit said in 2025 that the US definition is not limited by customary international law. Other countries are moving too. Britain boarded the tanker Smyrtos in June 2026, and its defence ministry said that once a vessel is found stateless Britain can use its domestic powers. A group of Nordic and Baltic states said in 2025 that vessels with no flag have no right to freedom of navigation. These are national positions, and other states have not all accepted them.

Follow what would happen to a harmless stateless habitat. If no warship cares, nothing happens at first. Then the indirect routes begin. Each person aboard remains a national of some country, which can reach them. The United States claims power over certain crimes by or against its nationals in places outside any nation's jurisdiction (18 USC 7(7)) and taxes citizens abroad under Cook v. Tait. Ports ask for the ship's papers. Insurance cover usually lapses when a ship loses its flag, according to the group Human Rights at Sea, and radio licences, safety inspections and crew documents normally come through a flag state. The tanker Sea Princess was struck off the Cook Islands register while at sea on its way to scrap, and its crew were left with no flag state responsible for sending them home. If a stateless vessel is robbed or rammed, no government is obliged to speak for it.

Reading the text, it seems that being stateless is not itself an offence under UNCLOS, and that a country needs its own law and some accepted ground before it can punish anyone aboard. The potential lies there, and it is small. The strongest version is a small vessel doing nothing else that any state prohibits, attracting no attention, with occupants who accept that they have no protection. It holds only as long as nobody chooses to act. Announcing a new country is what draws attention, as the XLII seastead off Phuket found in 2019 when Thailand charged its occupants, and that was a structure inside a coastal zone.

odds.why: Taking an unregistered boat to sea is easy, so the chance of getting there is fairly high. Article 110 expressly allows any warship to board it, and courts in several cases have treated such vessels as having no protection. How far a state may go after boarding is still argued, which leaves a little legal room. Insurers, ports and banks generally depend on a flag, so money and holding on score low.

rules.says: A ship sails under one flag and answers to that state on the high seas. One using flags as it suits may be treated as having none.
A warship may board on reasonable suspicion that a ship has no nationality, check papers and search further. It says nothing of seizure or prosecution.
For piracy and illegal broadcasting the treaty does give powers of seizure and arrest, which is the contrast writers point to.
Freedom of the open sea protects ships entitled to a state's flag. A vessel without one could claim no state's protection.
Stateless vessels on the high seas fall under US drug law with no link to the United States needed.
US definitions of a vessel without nationality, and the 2008 crime of operating an unflagged submersible to evade detection.

zones.name: A fixed or tethered platform on the high seas
zones.essay:
The idea here is a platform that stays in one place on the open ocean, far beyond any country's coastal zones, either standing on the sea floor or held by a very long mooring. It combines the high seas with the kind of structure used for oil and for old sea forts. The legal attraction is a question the treaties do not answer directly, which is whether such a thing is a ship at all. Founders hope that if it is no ship, the rules on flags and boarding will not touch it.

Some of this is clear. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says in Article 87(1)(d) that freedom of the high seas includes the freedom "to construct artificial islands and other installations permitted under international law, subject to Part VI". Part VI is the continental shelf chapter. So a structure standing on seabed that belongs to a coastal state's shelf falls under that state, through Articles 60 and 80. Article 87 opens by saying the high seas are open to "all States", and writers read these freedoms as belonging to countries, so a private person uses them through a country. Article 89 says no state may claim any part of the high seas. Article 121 says an island is "naturally formed", which excludes anything built.

What is open is the classification. UNCLOS does not define "ship", as Wangwang Xing and Ling Zhu note in a 2021 study, and definitions differ between treaties and national laws. They propose a test based on function, under which floating offshore systems count as ships while they are navigating. Olivier Lasmoles writes that platforms are not ships unless they have propulsion or navigation systems, and he reports Alfred Soons's three types of artificial island, namely anchored floating platforms, fixed seabed structures and concrete constructs. National law pulls in different directions. Richard Shaw, writing in 2000 about the floating oil production vessels called FPSOs, explains that English courts ask whether a thing is "used in navigation", and that one staying at an oil field for years probably does not qualify, while an Australian statute covers structures that can float and be moved as a unit. A working group of the international oil pollution fund concluded that a moored FPSO carrying no oil as cargo is not a ship for its purposes. Panama offers a practical example. When Ocean Builders asked it to class MS Satoshi as non-seagoing, Panama refused because the ship had an engine and a flag.

Reading the text, it seems that Article 110 may not fit a true fixed platform. It lets a warship board a "foreign ship". Article 109 on illegal broadcasting speaks separately of "a ship or installation" and of "the State of registry of the installation", so the drafters knew the difference and also expected that an installation might have a registering state. That reading gives the founder less than it first appears. The rule that protects a ship from boarding, exclusive flag jurisdiction in Article 92, also speaks only of ships. A structure outside Article 110 would also appear to be outside Article 92, so no treaty article would stop a warship from coming aboard, and the structure would have no state to object. No court has ruled on this. Louis McDonough Monroy of Ghent, discussing a 2023 proposal, concludes that such a structure would either come under the state that registers or deploys it, or be stateless, in which case all states could potentially enforce their laws against it. The Sealand litigation gives no answer, since the fort stood on seabed near Britain and later came inside its territorial sea.

The next question is the sea floor. Most of the open ocean lies over the deep seabed, where Article 137 says no person may take any part as their own. The treaty does not say plainly whether a long-term mooring there needs anyone's permission, and it gives no title to the ground. The International Seabed Authority's powers cover exploring and exploiting resources (Article 1(1)(3)), so a mooring for housing appears to be outside its licensing. The BBNJ Agreement, in force since January 2026, requires its members to assess activities under their control in these waters, which reaches a founder only through a member state.

Follow it through. A group charters a tow from a port, and the tug has a flag and an owner. Published estimates start at about $50 million for a small deep-sea platform, and insurers would ask who regulates it. MS Satoshi's owners, with a real flag and a stationary ship in a calm gulf, said the nearest offer of liability cover was a $1 million premium for $5 million of cover. The Aisland barge off Dubai broke in two in a wave in February 2024 and three people died. Supply boats carry their own flags and call at ports where they can be pressured, as Britain and Sweden did to the suppliers of radio ships. The residents stay nationals of their home countries, which tax them and may reach crimes committed in places beyond any nation's jurisdiction, as the United States does under 18 USC 7(7). Banks would look for a regulator and find none. Del Complex, an American company, said in 2023 that its computing barges would "operate as sovereign nation States", and how far that went is not known.

The potential is that this is one of the few places where no coastal state holds title and the classification really is unsettled, so a founder could present a respectable legal argument. The strongest version registers the structure with a real state, as Article 109 contemplates, and stands on deep seabed beyond every shelf. It would then be governed by that state's law, which gives stability and removes independence. Without a state, it would rest on the argument that no rule yet addresses it, and that argument would be tested the first time a navy took an interest.

odds.why: A platform in deep water costs at least about $50 million and has to survive open-ocean waves, which sank Aisland, so building scores low. The law scores somewhat better than a plain stateless boat because no treaty clearly says what such a structure is, although Article 89 still bars any claim to the sea. Holding on is low because no state would have a duty to protect it. Its supplies, insurers and residents can all be reached from land.

rules.says: High-seas freedoms include building artificial islands and other installations permitted under international law, subject to the continental shelf rules.
Exclusive flag jurisdiction and the limits on boarding are both written for ships. Whether a fixed structure counts is not stated.
Refers to 'the State of registry of the installation', showing that installations may have a registering state.
Artificial islands and certain structures on a coastal state's shelf fall under that state.
No person may take any part of the deep seabed as their own.

zones.name: A ship under the flag of an unrecognised or non-treaty state
zones.essay:
A founder may think of avoiding the ordinary register by flying the flag of a place outside the usual system. That could be a country that has not joined the Law of the Sea treaty, a real government that most countries do not recognise, such as Taiwan or Somaliland, or a self-declared micronation such as Sealand. These three cases sound alike and are treated very differently, so it helps to take them one at a time.

The first is easy, and the law is clear. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, has 172 members, and the United States is not one of them. American ships sail freely. Article 90 says "every State" may sail ships under its flag, and rules such as flag nationality and the right of visit are older than the treaty, appearing in the 1958 Convention on the High Seas that the Marino-Garcia court applied, and they are generally treated as customary law, which binds countries whether or not they signed. A ship from a non-party state is therefore an ordinary ship. Staying out of the treaty gives no freedom from boarding, and it gives no weaker flag.

The third case is also fairly clear, in the other direction. Article 91 says "every State" sets the conditions for its nationality, and a ship has the nationality of "the State whose flag they are entitled to fly". A court in Cologne held in 1978 that Sealand has no real territory, population or effective government. A flag issued by a place of that kind would appear to give no protection. The treaty does not mention unrecognised flags by name, so this is an inference, but it has strong support. In Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine in 1948 the Privy Council refused protection to a ship flying a Zionist flag, saying freedom of the sea belongs to ships entitled to the flag of a state. American law treats a vessel as without nationality when the named country denies the registry. A micronation's own confirmation would be unlikely to satisfy anyone, because the officer is looking for a state. Writers such as Eduardo Cavalcanti de Mello Filho say falsely flagged ships are stateless and any state may enforce its laws against them.

The middle case is the open one. Neither the treaty nor any court says how many recognitions make a "State" for Article 90. Taiwan is the working example. It has a real government and a ship register, and only a small number of countries recognise it. The 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement found a way around the problem by creating the category of "fishing entities". A 2020 thesis by Po-Hsiang Liao at National Taiwan University finds that in regional fishing bodies with boarding systems, notices from other states about Taiwan-flagged vessels are treated as accepting Taiwan's inspection role and its exclusive authority over those vessels. Ying-Ting Chen's 2014 Southampton thesis describes the same arrangements as raising real ambiguities. So Taiwan's flag is accepted through practice and through organisations, with no treaty giving it a general answer. Anne Hsiao's 2011 comparison of Taiwan and Northern Cyprus finds that lack of recognition weakens an entity's legal position without making it legally non-existent, that states deal widely with an entity whose existence broke no international law, and that an entity born from an unlawful act faces collective non-recognition. A flag from Northern Cyprus would be weaker than one from Taiwan for that reason. That last step is reasoning from her comparison, and her abstract does not address ships.

Somaliland shows the question at its sharpest. Israel recognised it in December 2025 after 34 years of self-rule, so one UN member treats it as a state. Whether it runs a ship register is not known. Reading the text, it seems that a Somaliland-flagged ship could expect to be treated as a national ship by a country recognising Somaliland, and might be treated as stateless by others, since Article 110 is applied by each warship's own government. No court has tested a flag that some warships accept and others do not.

Follow what happens to a ship under such a flag. Port officers inspect a ship's documents at each call, and it appears that a flag few governments accept would raise questions every time. Insurance is the next test. MS Satoshi's owners, flying Panama's flag, could not get usable liability cover, and they found that no insurance meant no crew, then no safety rating, then no flag. Registries such as that of the Marshall Islands handle ships' radio licences, and only member countries of the International Telecommunication Union can apply for frequencies, so a place outside that union has no route to either. The nationals aboard remain under their own countries' law.

The potential is real only for the middle case, and it belongs to the government concerned. An unrecognised government that already runs ports and courts can build acceptance of its flag slowly through practice, as Taiwan has. A founder could at most register a ship with such a government and accept its law, which gives no more independence than an ordinary flag and less protection. The strongest version would be a ship under the flag of a government with some recognition, trading only with states that accept it, while the question stays unanswered everywhere else. A private founder's own flag stands far below that, and the cases give no support for it.

odds.why: Painting a flag on a ship is easy. The legal score is low because courts and states look for a state behind a flag, and a micronation's flag would appear to offer nothing. Taiwan shows that an unrecognised government's flag can work through long practice, but that belongs to a real government and cannot be copied by a founder. Insurers and ports work with recognised flags, so money and holding on are low.

A warship may board on suspicion of no nationality, and each government decides for itself which flags it accepts.
A flag with no state behind it gave a ship no protection.
Created 'fishing entities', which lets Taiwan take part in high-seas fishing bodies without being treated as a state.

zones.name: Dealing with a flag registry run by a private company
zones.essay:
Many people are surprised to learn that some national ship registers are run by private companies, sometimes on another continent. A ship flying the flag of Liberia is registered through a company based in Virginia. That raises an obvious thought for a founder. If a flag is a service sold by a company, perhaps a founder could negotiate with that company, or set up one like it for a small country, and obtain a flag on special terms. The idea combines an ordinary flag, a deal with a host government and a business arrangement.

The history explains how this came about. Liberia's register began in 1948 under President William Tubman with the help of Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, and the first ship, the World Peace, was registered in March 1949. The International Trust Company ran it until 1999, when Liberia's government appointed the Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry (LISCR), a Delaware company based in Virginia, to manage the register and collect the fees owed to the state. That appointment rests on an Act of the Liberian Legislature. The register brings in roughly $24 million a year, and in the 2007-08 budget it was about six percent of government revenue, while during the civil war maritime money was about 70 percent. International Registries, Inc. of Reston, Virginia, descends from the original Stettinius company. It moved its business to the Marshall Islands after, according to one account, Charles Taylor demanded too much money. The Marshall Islands government started its register in 1988, and International Registries provides its administrative and technical support, including vessel registration, inspections, seafarer documents and radio licences.

The law on who holds the power is clear. Article 91 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says "every State" fixes the conditions for its nationality and that ships have the nationality of the state whose flag they may fly. A company can process the paperwork and collect fees, but the nationality comes from the state. Article 94 places the duties of supervision on the state as well. Open registers are generally accepted as lawful, and the writer Eduardo Cavalcanti de Mello Filho treats that as settled, while noting that a small state can be a responsible flag. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held in the M/V Saiga (No. 2) case that the genuine link requirement in Article 91 gives other countries no criteria for challenging a ship's registration.

Some things are open. Whether a third state may refuse to respect a flag whose government knowingly lets ships evade supervision is unsettled. Mello Filho calls these "flags of deceit", and he argues that the Saiga reasoning is thin and that non-recognition may be available. The Tribunal's approach suggests the only remedy is to report the problem to the flag state under Article 94(6). So a registry that exists mainly to sell cover may stay valid on paper while other governments test how far they can ignore it.

Recent events show how far a state can hand this work over and what can then go wrong. Gabon authorised a UAE-based firm, Intershipping Services, to run its register in 2018. By 2024 it was the fastest-growing by tonnage, and the EU and Britain sanctioned the firm in July 2025. Comoros withdrew authority from private operators and brought certificate issuance back in house. Cameroon expelled the tanker Smyrtos from its register in May 2026, and Britain boarded it the next month. Earlier, Sweden pressed Nicaragua into withdrawing the registration of the Radio Nord ship. In each case the state's decision was the one that counted.

Follow a founder through this. The ordinary route is available. A company formed for the purpose applies, the ship passes vetting on age, condition and owner, the owners are screened against sanctions lists, and the fee is paid. The result is a normal flag with that country's law on board and no special status. Reading the text, it seems nothing in Article 91 would prevent a small state from writing a statute that offers a special class of register for residential platforms, or appointing a founder's company as its registrar, as Liberia and Gabon appointed theirs. That would need a government and a legislature willing to act, and the registry company itself could not offer it. It would also bring the founder's company under the law of wherever it is based. Companies in Virginia answer to American courts and sanctions rules, and Liberia's statute limits LISCR's investors to US nationals.

The deal would be weak in the ways that matter most to a founder. A government that grants a registry contract can end it, as Liberia did in 1999, and a change of president could change the terms. Pressure from a powerful state tends to arrive at a small government's door. MS Satoshi's owners asked Panama to class their ship as non-seagoing, which would have lifted most treaty duties, and Panama refused. The flag would also carry its treaty obligations on safety and crew, since a state cannot contract those away by private agreement. A special class that left a ship with no real supervision would risk being treated as a flag of deceit.

The strongest version is a small state that passes a real law, supervises real safety standards, and contracts a founder's company to do the administration in return for fees that matter to its budget. No founder is known to have done this. Liberia shows that the money can matter a great deal to a state's budget, which gives a government a reason to agree, and it also shows that governments sometimes squeeze a registry for revenue. It would give stability and a say over the paperwork. Sovereignty would remain with the state that owns the flag.

odds.why: Registering with a company-run flag is routine, so the ordinary version is easy, and these figures are lower than for a plain registered ship because they assume a founder wants special terms. The company has no power to grant them, since nationality comes from the state. A small state could legislate for a founder, but no one is known to have achieved it and a later government can cancel it. Recognition is close to nothing because the flag state keeps the sovereignty.

rules.says: Each state sets the terms of its flag, and there must be a genuine link between state and ship.
The flag state must keep a register and supervise safety, crew and social matters. Art. 94(6) lets another state report failures to it.
The genuine link rule gives other states no criteria for challenging a ship's registration, as reported and criticised by Mello Filho.

zones.name: A habitat that keeps moving between ports and through coastal waters
zones.essay:
This idea avoids building anything fixed. A community lives on a ship that never stays long in one place, sailing across open ocean, passing through countries' coastal waters and calling at one port after another. It combines a flagged ship with the rule that lets ships pass through a country's waters, called innocent passage. The hope is that a home in constant motion never settles under any coastal government for long enough to be governed by it.

Much of this is settled and in the founder's favour. A ship under a real flag is lawful, and Article 90 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives every state the right to sail ships on the high seas. There, under Article 92, the ship answers only to its flag state. No treaty limits how long a ship may keep sailing. A moving ship also avoids the main rule that stops platforms. Article 60 gives a coastal state control over artificial islands and structures in its 200-mile resource zone, and a ship passing through is not one of these. Article 58 keeps the freedom of navigation in that zone for all countries. MS The World has worked this way since 2002, with residents who own their apartments and elect an advisory board, under the Bahamian flag.

The rules become tighter near a coast. The territorial sea is the belt up to 12 nautical miles from shore, where a country has full authority apart from the right of innocent passage (Article 17). Passage has a specific meaning. Article 18 says it means sailing through without entering port, or going to or from a port, and that it "shall be continuous and expeditious". Stopping and anchoring count only when they are a normal part of navigation or forced by distress. Article 19 lists what makes passage not innocent, including loading or unloading any person or goods contrary to customs or immigration laws, research, launching aircraft, and "any other activity not having a direct bearing on passage". So innocent passage is a right to cross. It is no basis for lingering, and it gives no right to live offshore in one spot within 12 miles.

Ports are the part most often misunderstood. A flag gives no right to enter a port. Ports lie in internal waters, and Article 25(2) recognises that a coastal state may set conditions on admission and act to prevent any breach of them. Women on Waves, whose Dutch-flagged ship carries a clinic, found this in 2004 when Portuguese warships blocked it. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression, but that ruling rested on human rights law. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of the ship docking. Once in port, residents and the ship fall under that country's law as well.

Some points are open. Women on Waves also raises the unresolved question of whether a ship that docks, boards a country's citizens and takes them out for an act banned at home is passing innocently. Whether a ship used as a permanent home, returning to the same waters again and again, stays within the words "continuous and expeditious" has not been tested in any known ruling. Reading the text, it seems that the passage rules look at what the ship is doing on each trip through the belt, and that a home on a real route would be treated like any passenger ship. A ship that repeatedly drifted just offshore for residents' convenience would look more like the stopping that Article 18 does not allow. A practical point follows from this. A ship registered as seagoing has to keep the certificates and crew that go with that, and a resident community may struggle to pay for them.

Follow one year of such a life. The flag state's law applies on board. Crew and safety rules follow the flag, under Article 94. Every landing is an immigration event. A resident has to hold a passport and any visa that each port demands, so a person without valid papers stays on board or is refused. Food, fuel and spare parts come from ports, and repairs from shipyards. The move-along approach gives no escape from tax, because a citizen's home country may tax regardless of where the person sleeps, as the United States does under Cook v. Tait. Banks ask for a home address and a tax residence. Medical care beyond the ship's clinic means going ashore. A child born on board usually takes nationality from the parents, and the 1961 statelessness treaty treats the birth as occurring in the flag country only to prevent statelessness.

The cases show that the money usually fails before the law does. Villa Vie Odyssey sold cabins from $99,999, and on 26 October 2026 in Sihanoukville its chief executive told residents to leave because the company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea Cruises cancelled its three-year voyage in 2023 without ever having a ship. MS Satoshi failed for a different reason, because it was meant to stay at anchor, and liability insurers would not cover a ship used that way. That suggests that continual sailing can be easier to insure than sitting still, though the cost of fuel and crew is far higher.

This route has more practical potential than nearly any other at sea, and it achieves less in sovereignty. The strongest version is a solid company or residents' association owning a well-maintained ship under a respected flag, on a real itinerary, with a private contract setting the internal rules. Such a community can last for decades and choose where it goes. Its members stay citizens of their own countries, its flag state can remove it from the register, and any port can refuse it. Having no territory also leaves it without a basis for statehood under the usual tests.

odds.why: People already live this way on MS The World, so building scores high. The law is favourable because a flagged ship is entitled to sail the high seas and pass through coastal waters. Holding is a little lower than a plain flagged ship because Villa Vie shows how fuel and money can end a community, and any port may refuse entry. Recognition is close to zero because moving gives no territory.

zones.name: A non-mining structure on the deep seabed
zones.essay:
The deep ocean floor beyond every country's continental shelf is called the Area, and an international body governs its mining. The idea here is to put something on that floor that has nothing to do with mining, such as a habitat, a research station or a data centre, and to argue that the mining body has no say over it. It combines the deep seabed with undersea habitats and the freedoms of the high seas. Each of these has its own rules, and they were written with different things in mind.

Start with what is settled. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says in Article 137 that no state may claim sovereignty over any part of the Area, that no state or person may "appropriate any part thereof", and that no such claim or appropriation will be recognised. So nobody can gain title to the floor, by building or in any other way. Article 141 opens the Area to use for peaceful purposes only. Article 135 says the water and air above keep their own status, which is high seas. An installation built for mining has "no territorial sea" and does not have the status of an island (Article 147(2)(e)), and research installations are treated the same way (Article 259).

The limits of the International Seabed Authority's power are also fairly clear from the words. Article 1 defines "activities in the Area" as "all activities of exploration for, and exploitation of, the resources of the Area". The Authority acts for humanity over those resources. Article 147(2), its rule on installations, covers those "used for carrying out activities in the Area". So a habitat that takes no minerals appears to be outside the Authority's licensing. Writers often move from that point to the conclusion that the habitat is free. That is the step the treaty does not make. The absence of an Authority permit requirement gives no permission, and Article 137 still applies.

Several questions are open. One is whether Article 87(1)(d), the freedom to build artificial islands and installations, reaches the sea floor at all. It sits in the chapter on the high seas, which is defined as parts of the sea (Article 86). The treaty does expressly allow one non-mining use of the deep floor, since Article 112 entitles all states to lay submarine cables on the bed of the high seas beyond the continental shelf. Reading the text, it seems that the cable rule shows that non-mining objects may lie on the floor, and the silence about anything larger may show either that such things are also allowed or that only cables were meant. No court has decided. A second open question is how permanent a structure can be before it counts as appropriating the spot. Article 137 forbids appropriation and does not define it. A cable that anyone can cross differs from a fenced habitat that excludes others, and reading the text it seems the second comes closer to what the article forbids, though that is an inference. A third is due regard. Article 87(2) requires high-seas users to have due regard for activities in the Area, and Article 147(3) requires "other activities in the marine environment" to show reasonable regard for them. A habitat placed inside a mining contractor's block could therefore raise a dispute, and the treaty gives no ranking of the two beyond that wording.

No one has built this, so the rest is reasoning from what the rules and real projects suggest. The closest real structures are in much shallower water and inside countries' zones. Aquarius is a permitted research station off Florida, Proteus is planned off Curaçao, and Ocean Spiral, a Japanese design for a deep undersea city, exists on paper. The deepest habitat in the record went to 610 feet, and the deep floor is commonly thousands of metres down. Autopia's small steel frame on the Saya de Malha Bank in 2002 stood in shallow water, and the seabed there is claimed as continental shelf. The Deepsea Ventures claim of 1974 is the nearest legal precedent. It claimed mining rights only, disclaimed any territory, and no court ever ruled on it.

Follow a project step by step. The work begins with a support ship, which has a flag, and with a port, which has a government. A project with American or European engineers comes under its home states' laws on exports and on licensing for those nationals. The BBNJ Agreement, in force since January 2026, requires its members to assess the environmental effects of activities under their control beyond national waters, so a sponsor in a member state would have to do that. The International Seabed Authority would not issue anything, which leaves investors and insurers with no document showing a right to be there. A lender cannot take a mortgage over ground that nobody can own. Air, power and food have to come down from the surface, so the surface link is the weak point. A person with a medical emergency faces a slow return, and if the habitat were kept at water pressure that person would need a long decompression first. Residents remain nationals of their home countries. If a structure counted as a ship or submarine, the flag rules would apply, and an unflagged one could be boarded under Article 110 if a warship could reach it. Whether a structure fixed to the floor counts as a ship has no settled answer.

The potential is mostly legal curiosity, because the engineering is far beyond what any private group has done. The strongest version would be a research installation sponsored by a real state, placed clear of mining blocks, publicly notified, and making no claim to the ground. Article 256 gives all states a right to conduct research in the Area, and Article 260 allows a safety zone of up to 500 metres around research installations. Such a station would operate under its sponsor's law. A version with no state behind it would have only the argument that no rule stops it, and it would hold no right to keep anyone away.

odds.why: Nobody has built a habitat on the deep floor, and the deepest on record went to 610 feet, so building is very unlikely. The International Seabed Authority's licensing appears not to reach a non-mining structure, which gives a small legal opening. Article 137 still bars owning any part of the floor, so a lender or insurer has nothing to rely on. Depth makes outside interference harder, which is why holding is not lower, but the surface supply link stays exposed.

rules.says: 'Activities in the Area' means exploring and exploiting resources, which sets the outer edge of the Seabed Authority's licensing.

Rules for mining installations. Other marine activities must show reasonable regard for mining.
Freedoms of the high seas, including building installations 'permitted under international law', and the right to lay cables on the deep floor.
All states may do research in the Area. Research installations have no island status and may have a safety zone of up to 500 metres.
Members must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control beyond national waters.

zones.name: Shallow banks beyond 200 miles and unresolved shelf claims
zones.essay:
Most of the open ocean is too deep to anchor in at reasonable cost, so founders look for places where the sea floor rises close to the surface far from land. The Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean is the favourite, a plateau of about 40,800 square kilometres, in places less than 33 feet deep, with its nearest land about 300 kilometres away. The idea combines open water above with a shallow bottom below, and it often relies on the fact that the seabed's status may be disputed or unfinished.

The treaty's basic rule separates the water from the floor. Under UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, water beyond 200 nautical miles from any coast is high seas. A coastal state's continental shelf, meaning its rights over the seabed, can reach further out if the geology qualifies (Article 76). Article 78 says those seabed rights do not change the status of the water above, and they may not cause unjustifiable interference with navigation. So a place can have high seas on top and a country's shelf underneath. Article 80 then applies Article 60 to the shelf, which gives the coastal state the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands, structures for economic purposes, and structures that may interfere with its rights, and sole legal power over them. Article 77 adds that shelf rights do not depend on occupation or on any express proclamation, so a coastal state that has done nothing there still holds them. Those points are settled. The 1970 American decision in United States v. Ray applied the same reasoning under the older treaty, stopping private builders on reefs off Florida.

Saya de Malha shows how uncertain the facts on the water can be. In 2004 the architect Wolf Hilbertz said most of the bank lay in the high seas, governed only by the Law of the Sea. Mauritius and Seychelles have since gone further. They filed a joint claim to extended shelf, which was endorsed in April 2011 according to the Commonwealth Secretariat, and on 12 March 2012 they signed a treaty to jointly manage about 400,000 square kilometres of seabed. A note from a 2022 scientific expedition says the claim was made to include the bank, that the seabed falls under joint management, and that the water stays high seas. Other sources are less exact. Wikipedia says Mauritius administers the whole bank because part lies in its 200-mile zone. A document from the southern Indian Ocean fisheries body shows Mauritius also asserting "historical rights" over the bank, and it does not state where the joint area's edge lies against the bank. So exactly which parts of the floor belong to the joint shelf remains unclear from public sources, although a founder should assume that the shallow parts are claimed.

The genuinely open questions concern places where shelf limits are not final. Article 76(8) sets a procedure under which a UN expert body, the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, makes recommendations, and limits set on that basis are final and binding. The Hatton-Rockall area in the North Atlantic shows how long this can take. Ireland, Britain, Iceland and Denmark for the Faroes all claim overlapping shelf there. Ireland and Britain settled their shared boundary in 1988. Ireland and Britain filed in 2009 and Denmark in 2010, Iceland has not filed, and the Commission will not review a disputed area without the consent of all concerned, so the submissions wait. The four have met since 2001 without agreement. In such a place everyone may agree that the seabed belongs to somebody while no one can yet say to whom. Reading the text, it seems that a founder gains little from this. Article 77 means that the rights exist before the limits are drawn, so whichever state turns out to own the shelf would have held authority all along. Several states would have reason to object at once, and none would be able to say the place was outside everyone's shelf.

A second open question is what kind of structure counts. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island". Article 60 catches every artificial island, but it catches other installations only if they have an economic purpose or may interfere with the state's rights. A moored vessel over the bank that flies a real flag and takes no resources might be argued to be neither, and to be exercising freedom of navigation, which Article 78 protects. Anchoring is ordinary in navigation, but a long-term mooring in one place looks more like a structure. No court has ruled, and a coastal state would likely argue the opposite. The 2019 raid on the floating home off Phuket shows how a government may respond, although that spot was inside Thailand's 200-mile zone.

Follow it through. The Autopia group sailed three days from the Seychelles in 1997 and returned in 2002 with a team that built a five-by-five-metre steel frame anchored to the bank, and then ran out of money, so its legal position was never tested. Samuele Landi planned to take barges there from Dubai, beyond the reach of extradition from Italy, and his barge broke in two in a wave in 2024 before he could leave. A real project would have to bring everything from Port Louis or Victoria or further, and those ports belong to the governments that claim the seabed. If those governments objected, the suppliers would be within their reach. Boats, insurers and banks would ask about permission. Nationals of the home countries stay under home law.

The potential is a physical base that is cheaper than deep water, and a legal situation where the water at least stays free. The strongest version is a flagged vessel, moored or anchored with the flag state's backing, doing nothing with the seabed, with the coastal states' knowledge or agreement. It could last as long as those states tolerate it. A more independent version would rest on the unsettled question of what a mooring is, and it would rely on two governments deciding to do nothing.

odds.why: A shallow bank makes anchoring cheaper, and two groups have aimed at Saya de Malha, but neither produced more than a steel frame. Water beyond 200 miles stays high seas, which helps a flagged vessel. The floor is usually claimed as extended shelf, and Article 60 then gives the coastal state control of artificial islands there. Those states run the nearest ports, so holding on is low.

zones.name: A new natural island beyond every coastal zone
zones.essay:
A volcano could one day push a new island above the sea far from any country's waters. This is the rarest situation in this list and one of the most interesting in law, because it would be real natural land, which an artificial platform can never be. The idea combines new land, the high seas and the old rules on unclaimed territory, with or without a state acting as sponsor.

Some parts are settled. Article 121 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says an island is a naturally formed area of land, surrounded by water, above water at high tide. A volcanic island meets that test, so it would avoid the problem that sinks every platform. Rocks that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life have no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf (Article 121(3)), though they do have a territorial sea, the belt of up to 12 nautical miles. The old rule on acquiring empty land is also well established. In the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, which must be completed by actual and continuing display of state authority. In the Clipperton award of 1931 France kept an uninhabited island on the strength of its 1858 proclamation and notice, because the island was empty and no earlier owner was proved. These rulings concern countries, and writers generally treat acquisition of this kind as a method used by states.

Nearly all new islands rise inside some country's waters, and then there is no question. Graham Island off Sicily in 1831 drew Sicilian and British claims within weeks and then wore away. Iceland said Surtsey was Icelandic as soon as French journalists landed on it in 1963. Beyond every zone the case has never arisen in any court, so the following points are open, and writers say so. Pawel Czubik's recent study separates three cases, an island under a state's sovereignty, an island on the high seas, and an island in zones of limited rights, which he calls the most problematic. For islands that can be treated as res nullius, meaning belonging to no one, he asks whether acts by private persons with no authority from a state can extend a state's territory. Duncan Hollis, writing about a new island near Tonga in 2006, said an island outside national baselines might be open to competing claims by discovery and occupation, and he raised the idea of treating it as common heritage. He said private groups may have a stronger claim to private property in such land than to statehood, and that their claims to found a nation rarely succeed today. A 1978 comment by Jimmy Verner asked whether seabed claims, nearness, occupation or discovery could support ownership of new islands in the Pacific.

The treaty text pulls two ways. Article 89 bars claims to the high seas, and Article 137 bars claims to the seabed beyond national limits. Neither article mentions land above water. On one view new land is simply new territory that the old rules can reach. On the other, it is a piece of the common seabed that happens to break the surface, so Article 137 forbids taking it. Reading the text, it seems that the second view has some force for the summit's roots and less for the dry part. A further difficulty follows. A state that took such an island would gain a 12-mile belt of territorial sea and its seabed, which would be carved from what had been high seas and common seabed, and the treaty does not say how those rules fit together. No state has had to answer that.

With a sponsor, the path is clearer. Suppose a state acts quickly, lands officials and governs the place. Under Palmas and Clipperton it has a recognised method, and rival states would need a better claim. A founder working with such a state could then receive whatever charter that state's law allows. Article 121 would give it territory, and that territory would belong to the sponsor, so the founder would hold a concession. The old US Guano Islands Act of 1856 is the closest private route. It lets American citizens claim islands with guano deposits for the United States, provided they belong to no other government. Leicester Hemingway relied on it for his raft New Atlantis, which was no island, and storms destroyed it. It too gives the claim to the sponsoring country and no independence to the finder.

Without a sponsor, the group would have real land with nobody's title on it, and a claim to statehood stronger than any platform's, since the Montevideo tests ask for a defined territory. It would still need other states' recognition, and states have shown little interest in giving it. Tonga annexed the Minerva Reefs in 1972 to stop a private country, and any coastal or nearby state could do the same by sending a boat. The landing party has to arrive from a port, which has a government. The group's members are nationals of states, and their taxes and criminal law follow them. There is no title that a bank could lend against, unless a government recognises one.

The ground may also disappear. Graham Island lasted about six months, Zalzala Koh about three years, and the Hunga Tonga island was largely destroyed seven years after it formed in 2015. Surtsey lasted because hard lava capped its ash, and that took years of eruption while the island could not be lived on. A founder would have to wait through all of this, with no water and little soil.

The strongest version is a group with a ship waiting, sailing under a state that has agreed in advance to back the group and to grant it a charter if land appears. This would be a very long wait, since no one can forecast the event, and new islands almost always rise inside coastal zones. It is the one sea route in which the land itself would meet the legal definition of territory. The chance is close to nil only because the event is so rare and the land so unstable.

odds.why: An island has to rise beyond every coastal zone and survive, and that has essentially never been tested, so building is very low. Natural land meets Article 121, which a platform cannot, and writers have treated such an island as possibly unowned. A state could claim it by occupying it, and a private group has no recognised way to gain title alone. These figures assume a private group, because with a sponsoring state the land would simply be that state's.

Discovery alone gives only a starting claim. Continuous display of state authority decides title.
France held an empty island on its proclamation and notice, because no earlier owner was proved.

zones.name: Building on a disputed low-tide feature in partnership with a claimant
zones.essay:
In disputed seas such as the South China Sea, several countries claim the same reefs. A private founder could not hold such a place alone, since rival navies are close by. The idea here is to approach one of the claimants and offer to develop a reef that dries at low tide, in return for a charter or a concession. The claimant gets a presence that supports its position, and the founder gets a protector. This combines reef law, a territorial dispute and a host government's grant.

Start with what the law says about the reef. A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water at low tide and under water at high tide (UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, Article 13). The International Court of Justice said in Qatar v Bahrain in 2001 that treaty law is silent on whether such features can be considered territory, and that state practice does not clearly allow or exclude taking them. In 2008, in the Pedra Branca case between Malaysia and Singapore, it held that sovereignty over South Ledge, a low-tide elevation, "belongs to the State in whose territorial waters it lies". In 2016 the panel in the South China Sea arbitration held that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". It also held that a feature is judged by its natural state before any building. China took no part and rejects the award, and an award binds only the parties, so its reach as a rule is argued over, though its reasoning is widely cited. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, which has no territorial sea (Article 60(8)).

Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore summarises the working position. A low-tide elevation within a territorial sea comes under the coastal state's sovereignty through its rights over the seabed. One beyond the territorial sea is part of the shelf, where the coastal state has rights over resources. In overlapping zones no state can claim sovereignty over such a feature, and which state holds the rights must wait for a boundary agreement. In the meantime states should make provisional arrangements and avoid unilateral acts.

So the founder's partner may not own what it is offering. The open question is what a permit from one claimant is worth while the zone is undelimited. Article 60 says the coastal state alone may authorise artificial islands in its zone. Reading the text, it seems that the permit is good if that claimant proves to be the coastal state and worthless, or a wrongful act, if it does not, and that nobody can say which until a boundary is agreed. The other claimants would treat the work as a violation at once. How a tribunal would treat a private investor who relied on one claimant's permit has not been tested in this setting.

A real example of a partnership of this kind is Layang-Layang, or Swallow Reef, in the Spratly Islands. Malaysian special forces put up a plaque in 1980 and built an encampment in 1983. Malaysia reclaimed land, raising the area from 6.2 to 35 hectares, and built a runway of 1,367 metres and a navy station. A dive resort operated there under Malaysian licence. China, Taiwan and Vietnam also claim the reef. On 6 January 2025 Malaysia revoked the resort's operating licence and it closed. The investor's position rested on one government's decision, and that government changed it. The example shows the business pattern. It says nothing about the reef's status in law, which would depend on its natural state before reclamation.

Tomás Cloma's Freedomland shows the private version of the idea going badly. He claimed part of the Spratlys in 1956 and asked the Philippine government for support. Taiwan's navy burned buildings there, and in 1974 the Philippines arrested him and made him sign over his rights. The partner he had courted took what he had claimed. The Minerva group in the South Pacific sought no partner, and Tonga annexed the reef in 1972.

Follow how the partnership would work. The claimant's law would apply, because that is the only source of the charter. Its navy decides who may land, and it may want the site for a garrison. Banks and insurers look at sanctions risk and war risk, and they would have to consider that a rival claimant regards the project as illegal. Other governments may warn their nationals off, since a home country's laws can reach its citizens. Workers need visas from the claimant, and their goods come through its ports. If shooting starts, the founder has no standing to negotiate. Under the South China Sea award's reasoning, a rival could later argue that the project sits on its seabed and demand its removal.

The potential is real but narrow. A founder could gain a physical base, a garrison next door and a commercial licence, as the Layang-Layang resort had until 2025. The strongest version would be a place where two claimants agree to joint development, so that the permit comes from both and the dispute is set aside, along the lines Beckman describes as a provisional arrangement. The Mauritius and Seychelles joint shelf is a peaceful model of two states sharing a seabed, though it is not a dispute over a reef. Independence is not on offer in any version, because the only thing that protects the project is a state's claim, and that state's interest is in strengthening its own position.

odds.why: Claimant states do build and license on such features, as Malaysia did at Layang-Layang, so building is plausible if a state agrees. The 2016 award says low-tide features cannot be taken by occupation, and a permit from one claimant is disputed by the others. Malaysia's revocation of the resort licence in 2025 shows how fast a partner can end the deal. Recognition is close to zero, since the partner wants the place for itself.

Sovereignty over a low-tide elevation belongs to the state in whose territorial waters it lies.

zones.name: Buying or inheriting an old structure such as Sealand
zones.essay:
A new founder might reason that Sealand has already done the hard part. It has been occupied since 1967, Britain has left it alone, and its family has issued coins and titles for decades. Perhaps the shortest route is to buy it or a structure like it, or to inherit one, and so step into a position nobody could build today. This idea combines an old platform with a purchase. The question is what a sale can actually transfer.

The law separates two things. One is ownership or possession of a structure, which a private person can have. The other is the authority to govern a place, which only states have and which is not sold with the structure. In the case of Sealand, the fort stood outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea when Roy Bates took it. In October 1968 a judge at Chelmsford held that a firearms law did not apply there, because Parliament had not extended it that far. James Grimmelmann, in his detailed legal history of Sealand, explains that the ruling is much narrower than the family claims. It says Parliament had not legislated for the fort, and it does not say Parliament could not. In 1978 a court in Cologne held that Sealand was no state, and no country has recognised it. On 1 October 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which covers the tower. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, allows that breadth (Article 3), and Grimmelmann calls the extension unproblematic under international law. Sealand claims a share of those waters, and he concludes that international law favours Britain on that. All of that was fixed before any buyer arrives, so a buyer would inherit a fort inside British waters.

The rest is less clear. Who holds title to the fort is itself uncertain. Britain abandoned the Maunsell forts in 1948, and Bates took Roughs Tower by occupation. Government lawyers concluded in the 1960s that a civil action to recover it would probably fail, and the Ministry of Defence offered him £5,000 to leave. A buyer would be purchasing possession and a contested history, and there is no land register that could prove a good title. Whether a British court would give effect to a sale or a will of the fort has not been tested. The family's mailing address runs through a British postbag. When Roy Bates died in 2012 his son Michael took over without any government stepping in, and he lives in England. Reading the facts, it seems that the inheritance worked because it changed nothing that Britain cared about, and that this is no sign that Britain accepted it as a succession to a throne.

The other uncertain matter is why Britain leaves the fort alone, because the tolerance is the real asset. A Cabinet Office meeting in November 1968 concluded that Bates was doing no actual harm and that force or special legislation was not justified. British policy since then has treated Sealand as a non-state. It has not removed the occupants since 1987. Tolerance of this kind was given to a particular family with a modest footprint, and a sale would change who it was being given to. Reading the facts, it seems that a buyer whose purpose was to host material or activity banned elsewhere would be asking the same government for a different decision. Britain's power to act against activities harming it is, in Grimmelmann's words, well established.

Real attempts show this. In January 2007 The Pirate Bay, a file-sharing index, tried to buy Sealand as a base after copyright pressure in Sweden. Between 2007 and 2010 Sealand was offered through a Spanish estate company, InmoNaranja, at an asking price of €750 million. No sale took place. Earlier, Alexander Achenbach invited the elder Bateses to Austria in 1978 to discuss a sale, and his associates seized the fort while they were away. The family retook it by helicopter. HavenCo, a data-hosting firm, was a tenant rather than a buyer, and it shows the risks of depending on the family. It promised customers protection from courts, it had about ten customers, and in 2002 the family took over the company and its servers.

Follow what a real sale would involve. The buyer pays money through a bank, which asks what is being purchased and from whom. The answer is a structure in British territorial waters, and tax and money-laundering questions follow in Britain and in the buyer's own country. A lender has no security. Insurers look at a wartime concrete fort that burned in 2006, and an RAF helicopter took the person aboard to hospital then, because Britain is the nearest authority. The buyer's staff need boats from British ports. If the buyer sold passports, the 1997 passport scandal shows what follows. Other old structures offer less. Most sea forts and platforms stand on someone's shelf or inside waters that have since been extended, and Article 60 requires disused installations in a coastal zone to be removed for safety. A disused platform that was never occupied has no such history behind it.

The potential is modest but real, and it is mainly a matter of name and history. A buyer gains a famous brand, a place people have heard of, a physical site and a very long record of being left alone. The strongest version would be a purchase from the family with continuity of the same low-key use, where no one is harmed in Britain and nobody tests the arrangement. That could continue for years. It would add nothing in law, because no title to govern was ever available from the seller.

odds.why: Only a handful of such structures exist and the Sealand family's last known asking price was €750 million, so a purchase is unlikely. A sale can pass possession at most, and the fort has been inside British waters since 1987. Holding on scores above the general platform figure because Britain has left Sealand alone for decades, but that tolerance went to one family doing little harm. Recognition stays below one percent, as no state has recognised Sealand in 59 years.

zones.name: A platform in a coastal zone with a permit and its own charter
zones.essay:
Most attempts to live beyond a state's reach have ended with a raid or a lack of money. This idea takes the opposite approach. A group asks a coastal country for permission to build a platform in that country's sea zone, and it also asks for a special law that gives the platform its own courts, tax rules or internal government. It combines the exclusive economic zone, which reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, with the zones that countries have carved out on land, such as the Dubai International Financial Centre.

The sea part of the law is clear. Article 60 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives the coastal state the exclusive right to build and to authorise artificial islands and certain structures in this zone. It also says that the coastal state "shall have exclusive jurisdiction" over them, including "customs, fiscal, health, safety and immigration laws". Artificial islands have no territorial sea and change no boundary (Article 60(8)). The state may set a safety zone of up to 500 metres around them (Article 60(5)). Beyond that, other countries' ships remain free to pass (Article 58). So a platform with a permit is entirely legal, and it remains within that country's authority.

The land part is also clear in principle. A country may pass a law setting up a zone with its own rules. Dubai's financial centre has had its own common-law courts since 2006. Próspera in Honduras ran on its own regulations, and it shows the danger. On 20 September 2024 the Honduran Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional with retroactive effect, and the company is now pursuing an investment claim against the state at a World Bank tribunal.

The open question lies where the two meet. Article 60 says the coastal state "shall have" exclusive jurisdiction. Reading the text, it seems that this is a statement of who holds power against other countries, and that nothing in it stops the state from using its own law to delegate daily functions to a local body, as it might for a port authority or a free zone. It is less clear whether a coastal state could promise never to apply its own criminal or immigration law to the platform. UNCLOS does not say, and no case has tested a charter of this kind at sea. A second open matter is classification. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island", so it is uncertain whether a moored floating platform falls under Article 60(1)(a) in every case or only under the rule for structures with an economic purpose. For a project with permission this hardly matters, because the state has authorised it either way. It matters if the state later revokes the permit and the operator argues that a registered vessel should be free to remain.

The nearest real attempt was planned for a lagoon, closer to shore than the offshore zone discussed here. On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seasteading Institute, and it cleared the way for studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, which would have needed legislation. Local residents objected and an opposition politician asked the government to withdraw. In February 2018 the government's position was reported to be that the deal had no legal force and had expired. Nothing was built. Oceanix Busan, a floating neighbourhood proposed off a South Korean port with the city and UN-Habitat behind it, claims no independence and had no residents reported, with about $200 million anticipated in 2021. Kiribati's president raised floating islands in 2011 and his government instead bought land in Fiji. XLII off Phuket in 2019 is the reverse case, a home placed without permission and raided by the Thai navy, with its occupants charged under a law carrying life in prison or death.

Follow how this would actually go. The founder needs a government willing to pass a law, and a law of this kind is usually a political fight, because voters ask what is being given up. Then come an environmental review, a construction permit, and rules on maritime safety for a structure that the classification societies may not have standards for. The host's own tax and immigration laws apply until the special law displaces them. Banks would look at the host's banking regulator, and this is a real advantage over any independent project, since correspondent banks, the banks that connect others internationally, have someone to rely on. Insurers can price a permitted structure. Staff and residents hold visas under the host's rules. Their home countries still reach them, and a host that has extradition treaties can hand them over. Children born there would take nationality under the host's law and the parents' law.

The largest risk is political. A later government can repeal the law, and a court can strike it down, as in Honduras. Investment treaties may pay compensation, though they do not bring the zone back. Article 60 leaves no neutral fallback, since sole legal power belongs to that same state, and a platform is easier to tow away or close than a town. Reading the text, it seems that a founder would be better protected by a treaty between the host and another state than by a contract alone, but a treaty needs a second government to care.

There is real potential here, more than in most sea routes, and it comes from giving up independence at the start. The strongest version would have a stable host with a tradition of special zones, a statute and constitutional change passed with broad local support, an arbitration clause and an investment treaty behind it, and local people sharing in the benefit, which French Polynesia lacked. It would have separate rules in many areas and remain part of the host country. That makes recognition as a separate state very unlikely, and it is not the goal of such a project.

odds.why: Article 60 lets a coastal state authorise a platform, and special zones on land show that a government can grant separate courts and tax rules, so the law scores well. Building is lower than for a zone on land because no state has yet agreed to this at sea, and French Polynesia withdrew in 2018. Holding is a little below land zones because a repeal or court ruling can end it, as in Honduras in 2024. Recognition is tiny because the platform stays within the host.

zones.name: A drifting iceberg on the high seas with no flag
zones.essay:
The idea here is to live on a large piece of drifting ice in open ocean, with no ship and no flag. This combines floating ice with the high seas, and it has a particular appeal in law. An iceberg is not obviously a ship, so the flag rules might not apply. It is not obviously land either, so the rules against claiming land might not apply, and it moves about on water that no state owns.

Very little here is settled. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, does not mention icebergs apart from a clause on ice-covered areas of a coastal state's zone. Its general rules still give some footing. Article 89 bars any state from claiming part of the high seas. Article 121 defines an island as "a naturally formed area of land", which reading the text does not appear to fit floating ice. Article 92 and Article 110, on flags and boarding, are written for ships. Whoever stands on the ice remains a national of some country, and nothing about ice changes that. Inside a coastal state's zone the position is different. Matthew Paterson, writing in 2019, suggests that a coastal state's rights over natural resources in its 200-mile zone cover icebergs, and Canada requires licences to harvest them in its waters.

What the ice itself is in law is open, and writers disagree. Mateusz Osiecki, writing in 2022, sets out three views of a free-floating iceberg. One calls it res nullius, belonging to no one and open to the first taker, in the way a fish is. Another says it may be held under a state's claim. A third calls it res communis, shared by all like the open sea. He argues that it is no country's property and sits on the high seas. That is one writer's reasoning, and no court has ruled on it. Even if a person may take a berg as property, as Osiecki's reasoning allows, property in a block of ice is a different thing from authority to govern people on it.

The one court to come near the question did so after a killing. T-3, or Fletcher's Ice Island, was a drifting block about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as an American research station. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla shot and killed the station manager there. The island lay in the sector Canada claimed, and Canada chose not to act. American officials flew him to Virginia and charged him under the law for crimes at sea, and in United States v. Escamilla (1972) the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether that law reached an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place. Congress settled the point for American law with a change in 1984. Both men were American and the suspect was taken home by his own government. So the case shows that a person on the ice does not fall outside all law, and it leaves the status of the ice itself unsettled.

Reading the text, it seems that a person on free-floating ice with no ship could say that no warship has the Article 110 right to board, because there is no ship. The reply is the same one that applies to fixed platforms. The rule that forbids boarding other than in listed cases also protects only ships. An unflagged camp on ice would have no flag state's exclusive authority behind it, and so no state would have standing to complain if another state's officers landed. No one has tested this. In practice the nearest state would be the one that supplies the camp, and it would not need to land to stop it.

Follow what would actually happen. The first need is an aircraft or a ship, which has a flag and a base in some country. Camp Barneo near the North Pole shows the pattern. It was a private camp, rebuilt from nothing each April, and every trip from 2002 to 2017 ran through Longyearbyen on Svalbard. When Chechen paratroopers exercised at Barneo in 2016 Norway imposed a flight ban. A dispute between Russia and Ukraine stopped tourist flights in 2019. The camp last operated in 2018, and no one had to board the ice to end it. Soviet and Russian drift stations show that people can live on floes for years, as North Pole-22 did for nine, with a government supplying them, and from the mid-2000s safe floes were hard to find. Antarctic ice has its own dangers, since A23a, once the largest iceberg in the world at about 3,500 square kilometres, was gone or nearly so by July 2026 after leaving cold water. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that bergs can roll over.

The money problems come next. A berg cannot be mortgaged in any meaningful way, as it may not exist in a few years, and no registry lists it. Liability insurers would have nothing to rate. Radio equipment needs licences from a state. Residents' home countries still tax and prosecute them, as Escamilla's case shows. A rescue depends on the nearest government's goodwill, and it ends in that government's territory. If the ice drifts into a coastal zone, as A23a did when it grounded 73 kilometres from South Georgia, a coastal state's rights come into play with no action by the residents.

The potential is limited, and it lies in the real legal uncertainty. The strongest version is a large, stable tabular berg in cold water, occupied by a small group with an aircraft or ship under a real flag, claiming property in the ice at most and no sovereignty. That would be a temporary station, lasting a season to a few years, with the supply ship's flag state as the practical authority. Declaring a state on it would add no rights.

odds.why: People have lived on drifting ice only with heavy state support or a season at a time, so a lasting private camp is very unlikely. The law scores a little because no court has settled what an iceberg is. Dropping the flag removes the protection a real ship would have, so it scores lower than ice with a state behind it. Flights and ships can be stopped from land, as Norway did at Barneo, and the ice itself melts.
