zones.name: Antarctica by nationals of non-treaty states and private parties
zones.essay:
The Antarctic Treaty has 58 members, which leaves most of the world's countries outside it. A treaty normally binds only those who join it. That raises a tempting thought. A person from a country that never joined, or a private company that is not a party to anything, might say that the ban on new claims does not apply to them. This idea combines the unclaimed and claimed parts of Antarctica with that gap.

Start with the treaty's words. Article IV(2) says that "No acts or activities taking place while the present Treaty is in force shall constitute a basis for asserting, supporting or denying a claim to territorial sovereignty in Antarctica or create any rights of sovereignty in Antarctica", and that no new claim may be asserted. Article VI applies this south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, with high-seas rights untouched. Article VII(5) makes each member give advance notice of expeditions organised by its nationals or from its territory. Article X says each member will "exert appropriate efforts, consistent with the Charter of the United Nations, to the end that no one engages in any activity in Antarctica contrary to the principles or purposes" of the treaty. The Madrid Protocol, an environmental add-on, bans mineral activity other than science and requires impact assessment. For members and those under their authority, these points are settled.

The first part of the idea has some truth. Whether the treaty binds outsiders is a real question in law. It is a general rule that a treaty creates duties only for those who accept it. The opposite argument is that a long-standing arrangement over a whole continent has become something all states must respect, sometimes called an objective regime, or part of customary law. Malaysia took a sharply different line at the United Nations from 1982, arguing that Antarctica belongs to the international community and questioning the right of the treaty's decision-making members to manage it, and Moritaka Hayashi records the General Assembly debates that followed. The treaty's members answered that their regime is lawful. No court has decided whether Article IV binds a non-member, and nothing suggests one will soon.

The second part of the idea does not follow from the first. Even if Article IV does not bind an outsider, that outsider still needs some other legal basis for gaining territory. Before the treaty, the method was occupation by a state. In its Western Sahara opinion the International Court of Justice treated occupation of empty land as a method used by states, and private persons have no recognised way of acquiring sovereignty by themselves. A non-member state could try to make a claim, and treaty members would refuse to accept it, since by Article IV(2) they cannot treat acts in the period as creating rights. Reading the text, it seems that a private person from a non-member country would therefore hold nothing either way, and the sentence "the treaty does not bind me" would remove one obstacle and leave the main one in place. The seven claimant states would also be free to regard the person as trespassing in a sector they claim, so far as they can reach them.

Now follow the indirect routes, which matter more. Almost every way into Antarctica runs through a member. Ships and flights usually leave from members such as Chile, Argentina, New Zealand and Australia, and members must give notice of expeditions from their territory. Article X then gives them a reason to obstruct. A departure port can refuse clearance. Britain requires a permit for anyone on an expedition organised in the UK or leaving from it, and for British-flagged ships. Norway fined the skipper Jarle Andhøy 45,000 kroner in 2014 for sailing to Antarctica without authorisation. Members can reach people through the nationality of crew, the place a company is registered, the flag of a ship and the location of its suppliers. A person holding a non-member passport on a ship flying a non-member flag, leaving from a non-member port, could in principle avoid this notice system. This route has never been tested by a settler, and it adds a very long voyage with no help close by. Reaching the coast also needs an ice-capable vessel and a crew willing to go, and their insurers are likely to ask about permits. Rescue would fall on the nearest station, and that government would then have the group in its hands.

Private parties from member states are a separate category, and they are clearly covered through their own governments. A private group can operate in Antarctica. Greenpeace ran World Park Base at Cape Evans, in the sector New Zealand claims, from 1987 until 1991 as the only non-government year-round base, and then removed it. Treaty governments officially ignored it, and New Zealand would have helped only in a life-threatening emergency. It claimed no land, and its aim was political influence at treaty meetings, which it had some success in. Westarctica and Flandrensis have announced states from home, and they have never been there.

The potential lies in the legal debate more than in any occupation. A non-member government might one day challenge the treaty's reach, as Malaysia did by argument. A private person gains little from that argument. The strongest version is a non-profit research or conservation camp organised through a member state with permits, which accepts the treaty, or else a privately financed non-member expedition that lands briefly, makes its point, and leaves. Neither would obtain land. Building anything lasting would need the money and logistics of a national program, with no mining allowed to pay for it under the Protocol as far as members are concerned, and the supply lines would run through the same members.

odds.why: Only governments and one Greenpeace base have kept year-round stations, and departure ports are mostly in treaty countries, so building is very unlikely. Article IV may not formally bind an outsider, which gives a small legal argument. That argument does not provide any basis for a private person to gain territory. Holding on is low because the nearest stations and claimant states are treaty members with a duty under Article X to act.

zones.name: Floating ice south of 60 degrees South
zones.essay:
Antarctic ice comes in forms that sit awkwardly across two legal systems. Land and attached ice shelves fall under the Antarctic Treaty, while the ocean around the continent is high seas under the law of the sea. A founder might look for the space between them, a large iceberg floating south of 60 degrees South, broken away from any shelf and arguably outside the treaty's reach. This idea combines floating ice with Antarctica and the high seas.

The starting text is Article VI of the Antarctic Treaty. It says the treaty applies "to the area south of 60º South Latitude, including all ice shelves, but nothing in the present Treaty shall prejudice or in any way affect the rights, or the exercise of the rights, of any State under international law with regard to the high seas within that area". Two things follow clearly. An ice shelf is inside the treaty, wherever its edge lies south of the line. And the waters south of the line remain high seas in the sense that states keep their rights there. For nationals of the 58 members, the rest of the treaty's machinery also applies, including notice of expeditions under Article VII(5) and, for parties to the Madrid Protocol, prior environmental assessment under Article 8.

The open question is what a free-floating iceberg south of 60 is. It is not named. It lies within "the area", which the treaty covers, and it floats on water where high-seas rights are preserved. Reading the text, it seems that either answer could be defended. Since Article VI first says the treaty applies to the whole area, Article IV's rule that acts cannot create sovereignty would seem to reach anything done there, including on a berg. The reservation about high seas protects the rights of states, such as navigation, and does not seem to create new rights to occupy ice. Writers have not settled this. Matthew Paterson, writing on icebergs in 2019, says the treaty excludes the high seas, which should be defined by UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Citing Christopher Joyner, he suggests that an ice shelf anchored to the seabed should be treated as land and otherwise as sea. Mateusz Osiecki argues in 2022 that a free-floating berg in Antarctic waters belongs to no country and sits on the high seas, and that taking and towing it would probably not breach any territorial rights. He was writing about a United Arab Emirates plan to tow ice for water, and the UAE has joined neither the treaty system nor UNCLOS. His reasoning concerns harvesting ice, and it goes no further than that. A towing ship still answers to its flag, and taking ice is a long way from founding a community on it. No court has ruled on any of this.

A further complication comes from claims. Seven states claim wedges of Antarctica, and Paterson writes of claimant states' 200-mile zones off those coasts, although Article IV has frozen the claims and the claims of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap. A berg might be in waters that a claimant regards as its own zone and that most other states regard as high seas. Whether ice counts as a mineral under the ban in Article 7 of the Protocol is another argument Paterson raises, with respect to harvesting.

History gives one striking example of what happens to things built on this ice. The Soviet base Druzhnaya I stood on the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf, and in 1986 the part of the shelf holding it broke off as the iceberg A23a. The base went with it, and a mission began in 1987 to save what could be saved. Debris could still be seen in the ice in January 2025. Reading those facts, it seems that the equipment stayed Soviet even though the ground under it had changed, and that a group of people would likewise remain attached to its home state. A23a shows the other danger too. It stayed stuck for years, then began moving in 2020, grounded 73 kilometres from South Georgia in March 2025, north of the 60 degree line, and by July 2026 it was gone or nearly so.

Follow a project through this. A group would need an ice-class ship or aircraft from somewhere. Most departure ports are in treaty countries, which must give notice and, under Article X, make efforts to stop activity contrary to the treaty. A member's national aboard needs a permit from that country, as Jarle Andhøy found when Norway fined him in 2014 for sailing there without authorisation, though he said he never landed. An iceberg moves, so a camp's position relative to the 60 degree line, and to any claimant's waters, changes without anyone's choice. A camp that crossed north of the line would leave the treaty area and become simply a camp on ice in the ocean, with fewer rules and much faster melting. Insurance, banking and titles have the same problems as on any ice, only more so, and rescue would fall on the nearest national program.

The potential here is that this is a real unanswered question in a system that usually leaves few. The strongest version is a scientific or campaign presence on a large tabular berg, under a real flag, with assessment done, and with no claim to the ice beyond possibly the property in what is collected. That may even be easier to justify than building on a shelf. It would last as long as the berg, a period that could be counted in years, and it would give no rights in the Antarctic system. A claim of sovereignty made from there would meet Article IV for treaty members and the general objections to private claims for everyone else.

odds.why: Only state programs have kept people on Antarctic ice, and a berg drifts, cracks and melts, so building scores very low. Writers disagree on whether a free-floating berg is on the high seas or inside the treaty's area, and no court has ruled, which leaves a small legal argument. Departure ports and rescue come from treaty countries. A23a shows that such ice can vanish within months of leaving cold water.

zones.name: Submersibles staying below the surface beyond national waters
zones.essay:
A submarine is hard to see. Some people imagine a community living in a large submersible that stays below the surface in open ocean, moving from place to place, unseen and so effectively outside government. This combines undersea living, the high seas and the question of flags. It helps to separate what the law says from what hiding can achieve, because they are different questions.

The law on the water is fairly plain. Depth creates no separate legal zone. The water column beyond national limits follows the high-seas rules, and under Article 87 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, all states may navigate there. Article 20 requires submarines and other underwater vehicles in a territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles from a coast, to travel on the surface and show their flag. No similar rule applies further out, so a submerged vessel on the high seas under a real flag is allowed, and its flag state's law applies aboard. UNCLOS does not define "ship", so treating a submersible as one is an inference, though Canadian law expressly counts submersibles as vessels, as the Canadian safety board noted in its report on the Titan. Article 110, which lets a warship board a ship suspected of having no nationality, would seem to apply to a submersible, once a warship has found it and it has surfaced or been stopped.

The United States has gone further for one kind of vessel. The Drug Trafficking Vessel Interdiction Act of 2008 (18 USC 2285) makes it a crime to operate or embark on a submersible or semi-submersible that has no nationality, beyond any country's territorial sea, "with the intent to evade detection". The penalty is up to 15 years in prison, and the law expressly applies abroad. A person charged has a defence if the vessel was lawfully registered, built to a classification society's rules, engaged in licensed commerce, research or exploration, or running a working tracking system. Congress's stated concern was drug trafficking and terrorism, but the words do not require drugs to be found. American appeals courts have upheld it. In United States v. Saac and United States v. Ibarguen-Mosquera the Eleventh Circuit rejected challenges to Congress's power, and in Valarezo-Orobio in 2011 it applied those rulings to a 35-foot semi-submersible that its crew scuttled near Malpelo Island. Whether other countries accept that this law may bind their citizens on the high seas when no link to the United States exists falls within the wider dispute about stateless vessels. That dispute is unresolved in international law, and the US cases rest on US constitutional law.

Reading the text, it seems that this statute reaches close to the idea discussed here. A long-stay unflagged submersible, built to avoid notice, is close to what Congress described, even if nobody aboard has done anything else. It would apply wherever American officers can reach the people concerned, including when they next come ashore in a country that cooperates. A registered and tracked submersible falls outside the statute, and it also gives up the advantage of being hidden.

The Titan shows how little a flag can matter until something goes wrong, and how much is then asked. OceanGate's Titan was not registered in any country and not classed or certified by anyone. OceanGate began registering an earlier hull in the Bahamas in 2019 and did not pursue it after learning the requirements. The dive site at the Titanic wreck lies beyond Canada's 200-mile zone. The support ship, Polar Prince, flew Canada's flag. After the fatal implosion in June 2023, investigators from Canada and the United States took up the case, and in 2026 the Canadian board recommended that Canada require submersibles operating with a Canadian support ship to meet safety guidance and that the guidance be made binding internationally. So an unregistered craft operated in open ocean for years with no regulator. Investigators could still reach the company and its support ship, because both had known addresses and countries.

Follow what long-term life would involve. Private submersibles today make dives lasting hours. Long-endurance submarines belong to navies, and the parts for them are tightly controlled exports. Any battery or diesel craft has to surface or reach a supply point often. Food, spare parts and crew changes come from ports or from a surface ship that has a flag and a registered owner. Radio use from under water is limited, and using radio at the surface needs a licence from a state. Medical emergencies mean surfacing and asking for help, and a rescue under Article 98 ends in a coastal state. A child born aboard would depend on the parents' nationality. Article 20 means any approach to a coast has to be made on the surface under a flag, and a coastal state may treat an unknown submarine in its waters as a security matter.

The potential is narrow. Hiding works for a while, and it gives no legal status. A hidden community has no way to bank, insure, trade openly or be recognised, because all of those depend on being known. The strongest version is the reverse of hiding, a registered and classed submersible or small fleet under a real flag, operating publicly from a registered support ship. Such a craft can stay on the high seas under its flag state's law, and residents could spend long periods below. It would be under that state's law and easy to find.

odds.why: No private group has lived for long in a submersible, and endurance without state resources is short, so building scores low. A flagged submersible is lawful on the high seas, but an unflagged one meant to avoid detection comes close to a crime under American law, which is why the legal score is low. Hiding makes holding on easier than for most projects until the next port call. A community that cannot be seen also cannot bank or be recognised.

rules.says: In a territorial sea, submarines must travel on the surface and show their flag.
High-seas navigation is open to all states. Nothing separate applies below the surface.
A warship may board a ship suspected of having no nationality.
Crime to operate an unflagged submersible beyond a territorial sea with intent to evade detection, up to 15 years, with defences for lawful registered or research use.

zones.name: A ship in the government service of a small state
zones.essay:
Ordinary ships can be boarded on the high seas in a few listed situations. Warships and certain government ships cannot be boarded at all. So a founder might think about a stronger form of the flag. A small state would own or operate a ship for government purposes, which would give it the highest protection the law of the sea offers, and a community would live aboard. No founder is known to have tried this, and the discussion below is reasoning from the treaty text and related cases. It combines the flagged ship with the idea of a host state making a special grant.

The law gives clear words. Article 95 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says warships on the high seas have complete immunity from the jurisdiction of any state other than the flag state. Article 96 gives the same immunity to "ships owned or operated by a State and used only on government non-commercial service". Article 110, the right of visit, expressly excludes ships entitled to that immunity. Article 32 says that nothing in the treaty affects the immunities of warships and other government ships operated for non-commercial purposes, with limited exceptions for the territorial sea. In the ARA Libertad case of 2012 the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ordered Ghana to release an Argentine navy ship that a Ghanaian court had held in port over a debt judgment. It called a warship "an expression of the sovereignty of the State whose flag it flies". So the protection is real and strong.

A warship is defined narrowly. Article 29 requires a ship belonging to a state's armed forces, commanded by a commissioned officer, crewed under military discipline, and listed in a service list. A private community does not fit.

Article 96 is more open, since it has two tests and neither is defined in the treaty. "Owned or operated by a State" might cover a ship chartered and run by a government agency. "Used only on government non-commercial service" is the harder test. The word "only" appears to exclude a ship that also sells cabins, charges rent or carries paying guests. Reading the text, it seems that a ship that serves as a home for a private community, paid for by residents, would fail, even if a state's name were on the papers. A ship used by a state as a research vessel, a diplomatic mission or a home for its own public servants would have a better argument. Whether people living aboard as a community can be part of "government service" has not been tested. No court is known to have addressed a residential case.

Even a successful claim brings a founder less than it seems. The immunity is from every state other than the flag state, and the flag state keeps full authority. The ship's master would answer to that government. Immunity in Article 96 covers the high seas, so entering another state's port or territorial sea would rely on other rules and on permission. The ARA Libertad shows both sides. The tribunal protected the ship, but the ship had first spent weeks held in port because a private creditor could go to a local court. Immunity protects the vessel and not the people once they step ashore. A resident who goes to a hospital in a port is under that country's law. Home countries still tax their citizens, as the United States does under Cook v. Tait, and a passport is unaffected.

Follow how a deal might work. A small state with a real need for income might agree to own a ship, because Liberia and others show that flag income can matter to a small state's budget. It would need a law, a budget entry and officials who actually control the vessel, because a ship that is operated by a private company in the state's name would look like a sham. Other governments can test that. Article 110(3) has a warship pay compensation if its suspicion proves unfounded, which suggests that a warship with doubts would still board. A powerful state unhappy with the arrangement could press the small state directly, as Sweden pressed Nicaragua over Radio Nord's registration. Insurers and banks would deal with the state. Money raised from residents to pay for the ship would undermine the claim that its service is non-commercial. Reading the text, a founder's interest and the legal test pull in opposite directions, since the more the founder controls the ship and profits from it, the less it counts as government service.

A related question is whether a non-state body with some international standing could do the same. Article 93 mentions ships on official service of the United Nations and certain agencies, under the organisation's flag. Nothing there covers a private founder. The Order of Malta keeps diplomatic relations with no territory, and its position comes from centuries of history that a new group cannot reproduce.

The potential is small and comes with a real price. The strongest version is a state-owned ship with a real public function, such as ocean research or disaster relief, staffed by public employees, on which private partners have contracts and no authority. That ship would be free of foreign boarding on the high seas. It would also be a government ship in every sense, so the community aboard would be living under that government's direct control. The community would gain protection from other states' warships and would lose its freedom from the state that owns the ship.

odds.why: Very few governments would own and run a ship for a private group, and no one is known to have achieved it, so building scores very low. If a real government does so, Article 96 gives strong protection on the high seas, which explains the high law and holding figures. The word 'only' in Article 96 means that residents paying for their homes would likely defeat the claim. Recognition stays low because the ship belongs to an existing state.

rules.says: Warships, and ships owned or operated by a state used only on government non-commercial service, are immune on the high seas from all but the flag state.
A warship belongs to the armed forces, under a commissioned officer and with a crew under military discipline.
The right of visit does not apply to ships with this immunity.
Ordered Ghana to release an Argentine navy ship. A warship expresses the sovereignty of its flag state.

zones.name: A pocket of high seas surrounded by coastal zones
zones.essay:
Coastal zones reach 200 nautical miles from shore, and in some enclosed seas those zones do not quite meet. They leave a pocket of open water that is high seas, ringed by one or more countries' zones. The Peanut Hole in the Sea of Okhotsk is the clearest example. It is about 55 kilometres wide and 480 kilometres long, more than 200 nautical miles from any coast, and surrounded by Russia's exclusive economic zone. A founder might see the attraction of such a place. It is high seas in law, and it is much closer to supplies than the middle of an ocean. This idea combines the high seas with the coastal zone around them.

Most of the law is clear. Under UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, water outside any state's exclusive economic zone is high seas (Article 86), whatever surrounds it. So in the Peanut Hole no state may claim the water (Article 89), ships from any country may sail, and a flagged vessel answers to its flag state (Article 92). Fishing fleets used this in 1991 and 1992, when many nations fished there, taking perhaps as much as a million tonnes of pollock, until China, Japan, Poland, Russia and South Korea agreed in 1993 to stop until stocks recovered. To reach the pocket a ship must cross the surrounding zone, and Article 58 keeps freedom of navigation through it for all countries.

The floor is where the idea weakens. In a place like this the seabed may belong to a coastal state as extended continental shelf, even though the water above does not. Article 78 says shelf rights do not change the status of the water. In November 2013 a UN subcommittee accepted Russia's argument that the Peanut Hole's seabed is part of its shelf, and in March 2014 the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf agreed with Russia. Since then the seabed and subsoil have been treated as Russia's shelf while the water remains high seas. Articles 60 and 80 then give Russia the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands on that shelf and any structures that have an economic purpose or may interfere with its rights. A founder who wanted something standing on the bottom would therefore need Russian permission, and a similar check is needed for any pocket, since a shelf can be extended under one even where nobody has yet acted. Under Article 77 those rights do not depend on occupation or proclamation.

What is left open is the same question that applies on shallow banks. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island" or say when a moored vessel becomes one. Reading the text, it seems that a flagged ship floating or drifting in the pocket is simply a ship on the high seas, and that the coastal state's seabed rights give it no power over that ship unless it harms the seabed. An anchor is more doubtful. Article 78 forbids unjustifiable interference with navigation, yet a long-term mooring is hard to describe as navigation, and a coastal state could call it a structure on its shelf. No case has tested this in a pocket. The surrounding state also has rights that apply very close by. Its fishing and environmental law applies once a vessel crosses into the zone, and Article 111 lets it chase a ship out onto the high seas for violations committed in the zone, which is called hot pursuit. In a strip only 55 kilometres wide, leaving the pocket for a day's sailing puts the vessel back under those rules for resource matters.

Follow what would happen. The nearest coast belongs to the surrounding state, and it is the natural source of supply and rescue. A project that relied on that country's ports would be under its customs and immigration rules at each call. A country that has surrounded a pocket has every reason to watch it, since it has already argued over the fish and the floor. Russia viewed foreign fishing there as a threat because the fish move between the pocket and its zone. Thailand's response to a small cabin off Phuket in 2019, though it was inside the zone, shows that a government can treat a mere announcement of autonomy as an attack on its sovereignty. Supply boats and aircraft from elsewhere would have to make long trips. The Sea of Okhotsk freezes in part in winter, and any platform would have to deal with that. Insurers, banks and the home countries of residents would respond here as they do anywhere on the high seas, and they would ask about the Russian seabed claim too.

Other pockets differ in detail, and a founder would have to check for each the state of any shelf claim, who surrounds it and how shallow it is. In a pocket ringed by several countries, each may have a shelf claim, and a project may meet a dispute of the kind seen at Hatton-Rockall. The general point stays the same. A pocket is high seas for ships, and it may well be someone's shelf for anything fixed.

The potential is that a flagged ship can lawfully sit in such a place, near land and supplies, and be on the high seas under its flag's law. The legal result is the same as on any other stretch of high seas, and Article 109 on illegal broadcasting still applies. The strongest version is a registered vessel, moving rather than anchored, with no interest in the seabed. It would be much more exposed to its neighbour than a ship in mid-ocean, and it would gain only convenience from being there.

odds.why: Getting a flagged ship into such a pocket is easy, but keeping a lasting community there is not, so building is low. The water is high seas, which gives a legal footing. The seabed may be a coastal state's, as with Russia's Peanut Hole since 2014, and that closes off anything fixed. One neighbouring state controls nearly every approach, so holding on is lower than on the open ocean.

rules.says: High-seas rules apply to all sea outside economic zones, territorial seas and internal waters, whatever surrounds it.
Shelf rights do not change the status of the water above.
The coastal state controls artificial islands and certain structures on its shelf.
A coastal state may pursue a ship from its zone onto the high seas for violations in the zone.

zones.name: A platform with a state that is losing its land
zones.essay:
Several low-lying Pacific countries expect rising seas to make their land hard to live on. They are real states with UN seats, large sea zones and few resources for adaptation. A founder might propose a partnership. The founder would finance floating or raised platforms in the state's own sea zone, and the state would grant a charter and its legal cover. If the land one day disappears, the platforms might be part of how the state continues. This combines a coastal zone, a host's grant and the idea of a state without ordinary territory. It has never been done.

The sea-zone part is settled. Article 60 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives a coastal state the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands in its exclusive economic zone, and sole legal power over them. So a small island state could lawfully permit a platform in its own waters. Article 60(8) also says such a platform is not an island and has no territorial sea of its own. In 2011 Kiribati's president Anote Tong mentioned floating islands, comparing them to oil rigs, at a cost of about $2 billion, and his government went on to buy land in Fiji instead.

The question of what happens to the state is moving quickly and is not closed. The usual test for statehood, in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, includes a defined territory. Pacific states have argued that a state continues even if its land is fully inundated, and that its zones continue. The Pacific Islands Forum issued a declaration on statehood in 2023. In its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change, the International Court of Justice said that loss of territory "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood", and that UNCLOS does not require states to update baselines once they are established. Judge Peter Tomka wrote separately that "territory has been indispensable to the concept of a State". On 24 September 2026 all 193 UN members adopted by consensus a political declaration that states a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, and says that states may keep their maritime zones once baselines are set. Harry Aitken, an Australian legal adviser writing in his personal capacity, describes this as a beginning, and the declaration's legal force and working details remain to be shown through what states do. Australia and Tuvalu signed a treaty in 2024, which he gives as the concrete step so far.

The reported texts do not address platforms. Reading them, it seems that continued statehood is grounded in the state's existing legal identity and in other states' agreement to keep treating it as a state. A platform would be useful for housing people and would not itself supply the missing territory, since Article 60(8) denies it island status. Whether a state whose only physical presence is a set of platforms in its own zone would be treated as the same state is an open question. The presumption in the 2026 declaration would help it. Tomka's view would count against it, and no court has decided.

Follow how the partnership might go. The first problem is consent. The declaration speaks of "mobility with dignity" and says that relocation must be voluntary. A foreign investor offering to build the future home of a nation, in exchange for a charter, is asking a small state and its voters to give up something sensitive, and the French Polynesia case shows that local opposition can end such a plan even when ministers agree. The second is money. Kiribati's figure of $2 billion came with the remark that other countries would have to pay. It appears that aid of that kind would reach the state first, so a private founder would depend on the government for it. The third is control. Article 60(2) gives the host fiscal and immigration power, and the host could revoke a charter later, as Honduras's court ended its zones in 2024. For the founder, the state's recognition is the main asset, and the founder cannot own it. The state's UN seat, passports, bank links and treaties are the state's own. The founder's residents would need to be the state's citizens or permitted foreigners, so the state's nationality law would decide who may live there. Tuvalu's own plan so far has been a digital archive of its land and culture and agreements with other countries that it stays a state, which suggests where its priorities lie.

The potential is higher than for other platform routes, in one specific sense. This is the one situation in which a platform would stand under a recognised state that has a strong reason to want it and whose continued existence other states have just promised to presume. Banks, insurers and ports would be dealing with a real government. The strongest version is led by the state itself, with outside finance on ordinary commercial or aid terms, with residents' consent, under the state's own law. What it cannot offer is a new country for the founder. The sovereignty would be that of the existing state. A founder seeking control would be asking that state to give up what it is working to keep, and the French Polynesia case suggests how local voters may respond. The recognition figure below refers to a new separate entity. The host itself already has recognition.

odds.why: No such platform exists, and Kiribati's 2011 idea came with a $2 billion cost and no funder, so building is low. Article 60 lets the state permit it, and the 2026 UN declaration presumes that such states continue, so the legal score is fairly high for a project under the state's own law. A later government or local opposition could end a founder's charter. Recognition here means recognition of a new separate entity, which is unlikely, because the host is already a state and has no reason to give that up.

rules.says: A coastal state may authorise artificial islands in its zone and holds exclusive jurisdiction over them. They are not islands in law.
Loss of territory would not necessarily mean loss of statehood, and UNCLOS does not require baselines to be updated.
A political declaration adopted by consensus, with a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise.
The usual test for statehood includes a defined territory.

cases.challenge: Forfeited under the Palestine Immigration Ordinance; upheld by the Privy Council
cases.recognition: Flag held to give no state's protection
cases.name: The Asya and Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine
cases.story: The Asya was a motor freighter owned by Naim Molvan, who was neither a citizen nor a resident of Palestine, then under British rule. On 27 March 1946 the British destroyer HMS Chequers sighted her on the high seas about 100 miles southwest of Jaffa. She was flying no flag. She later raised a Turkish flag, and when the boarding party came near she hauled it down and raised a Zionist flag. She did not answer a signal asking where she was going. She had no passenger list and no normal ship's papers, and charts showed a course from France to a point near Tel Aviv. She was taken to Haifa with 733 people aboard, none with a passport or visa. The passengers were landed and sent to a clearance camp. The District Court of Haifa ordered the ship forfeited under the immigration law, and the Supreme Court of Palestine agreed. The owner appealed to the Privy Council in London, then the final court for the British Empire. He argued that the seizure happened on the open sea and broke international law. The court answered that freedom of the open sea is a freedom of ships that fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a state within the community of nations. The Asya met neither condition, so no question of international law could arise in its favour, and it "could not claim the protection of any State". The case is still cited because the flag at issue was a flag of a people and a movement, with no state behind it at the time. It is the nearest old authority for what a self-made flag does at sea. The reasoning was given in a colonial immigration case before UNCLOS existed, and how far it reaches today is part of the current argument over stateless vessels.
cases.mechanism: A flag protects only when a state stands behind it. A vessel under a flag of no state has no one to object when it is stopped and seized.

sources.t: Naim Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine (The Asya), Privy Council 1948, Refworld

cases.stopped_by: US Coast Guard cutters Dependable and Lipan
cases.challenge: Convictions upheld by the Eleventh Circuit
cases.name: United States v. Marino-Garcia (the Four Roses)
cases.founder: Crews of the Four Roses and the Lady Mark
cases.story: United States v. Marino-Garcia is a 1982 decision of the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, joined with a second case, United States v. Cassalins-Guzman. It is the usual starting point in American law for what a country may do to a stateless vessel. The Coast Guard cutter Dependable approached the Four Roses on the high seas about 65 miles off Cuba and 300 miles from Florida. She carried about 57,000 pounds of marijuana and nine foreign crewmen, and nothing showed the cargo was meant for the United States. The court treated her as stateless. She had once been registered in Honduras, but when stopped she showed no Honduran authority, her name had been altered, and "Miami, Florida" was stencilled on her bow. In the second case the cutter Lipan found the Lady Mark near Cuba with about 20,000 pounds of marijuana and four national flags aboard. The trial judge had dismissed that indictment because nothing linked the vessel to the United States. The appeals court upheld the first convictions and reversed the dismissal. It held that American drug law reached stateless vessels on the high seas and that international law permitted this with no connection to the United States. It called such vessels "international pariahs" with no internationally recognised right to navigate the high seas, and "floating sanctuaries from authority". It said commentators had unanimously agreed that all nations may assert jurisdiction over them. That statement is less secure today. Writers now divide between an "any state" view and a "nexus" view, and some argue that the right to board does not bring a right to prosecute. The case binds courts in one part of the United States, and no international court has endorsed it.
cases.mechanism: American courts treat statelessness as enough to apply US criminal law to foreigners at sea, with no link to the United States.

cases.stopped_by: Royal Marines and British law enforcement
cases.challenge: Captain arrested and charged under British sanctions law; outcome not known
cases.recognition: Cameroon had expelled the ship from its register in May 2026
cases.name: Interdiction of the tanker Smyrtos
cases.story: On 14 June 2026 Royal Marine Commandos and specialist officers boarded the oil tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel. She was carrying more than 100,000 tonnes of Russian crude and flying the flag of Cameroon, which had expelled her from its register that May. Her Indian captain was arrested and charged with controlling a ship delivering prohibited oil from Russia to a third country. It was described as Britain's first solo interdiction of a sanctioned tanker. Britain relied on Article 110 of UNCLOS and on its own law, and its Ministry of Defence said that "where a vessel is determined stateless, the UK can exercise powers available under its domestic legislation". Accounts of the location changed. Early government statements said the boarding took place on the high seas. Later ones said the ship had entered British waters, and the prosecutor said it had entered British territorial waters "without a legitimate flag". That matters, because a country has full authority inside its own territorial sea and a much weaker claim outside it. The case belongs to a wider run of actions against the so-called shadow fleet, tankers that use opaque ownership and false flags. The United States seized the Marinera, formerly Bella 1, with British support and rejected her claimed Russian registration. It also boarded the M Sophia after she allegedly claimed Panamanian registry falsely. In June 2025 a group of Nordic and Baltic states said vessels without a valid flag have no right to freedom of navigation. Thea Coventry of Leiden University argues that if the boarding took place on the high seas, Britain would need a basis such as universal jurisdiction, and that oil deliveries fall outside its accepted scope. She also suggests that repeated acts of this kind could shape a future customary rule if other states stay silent. How the prosecution ended is not known.
cases.mechanism: A ship struck off its register becomes open to boarding, and states are now testing how far they can go after that under their own sanctions law.

Addleshaw Goddard, Legal framework: flag State jurisdiction and statelessness
Rodriguez, How stateless vessels challenge maritime order under UNCLOS, Maritimes Crimes, Feb 2026

cases.name: Del Complex BlueSea Frontier Compute Clusters
cases.story: In 2023 a company called Del Complex announced what it called BlueSea Frontier Compute Clusters, computing centres on barges placed on the high seas. It said it wanted them to "operate as sovereign nation States", and it cited UNCLOS and the Montevideo criteria, the four tests usually used for statehood. No specific site is known, so the coordinates given here are only a marker for the open Pacific. Whether any barge was ever built is not known. Louis McDonough Monroy, a doctoral fellow at the Maritime Institute of Ghent University, examined the plan on the International Law Blog in November 2023. He pointed out that Article 87 of UNCLOS gives the freedom to build artificial islands on the high seas to states, with due regard for others. If the barges are self-propelled they might count as ships, and a ship must fly one state's flag and answer to it. A ship with no flag, or with several, is stateless and open to the right of visit under Article 110. He read Articles 208 and 214 as assuming that some state holds authority over such structures. His conclusion was that the barges would either come under the sole authority of one state or be stateless, in which case all states could potentially enforce their laws against them. On statehood he noted that state practice rejects sovereign claims on the high seas, and he gave Sealand as the example of a platform no state has recognised. He called the plan short-sighted and suggested that registering in a sympathetic country would serve the company better.
cases.mechanism: A company announced sovereign computing barges on the high seas. The legal analysis found it would either answer to one state or have no protection from any.

sources.t: McDonough Monroy, Floating sovereign tech island paradises?, International Law Blog, 13 Nov 2023

cases.recognition: Recognised by few states; flag accepted through practice and fishing bodies
cases.name: Taiwan's ship flag and the 'fishing entity' arrangement
cases.story: Taiwan has its own government, its own ports and its own ship register, and most countries do not recognise it as a state. That makes it the most useful real example of a flag whose legal footing is uncertain. UNCLOS says every "State" may sail ships under its flag, and it does not explain what happens when a government's statehood is disputed. Fishing brought the question into the open, because high-seas fish stocks cannot be managed if a large fleet stays outside the rules. The 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement allowed "fishing entities" to take part in the regional organisations that manage those stocks. Taiwan's participation in each organisation rests on an arrangement between Taiwan and that body, which sets out what it may and must do there. Two academic studies describe the result. Ying-Ting Chen's 2014 doctoral thesis at Southampton says that since fishing entities are not states, their role raises ambiguities, especially over enforcement at sea. Po-Hsiang Liao's 2020 master's thesis at National Taiwan University asks whether any legal instrument formally gives fishing entities the exclusive power of a flag state. He concludes that in organisations with boarding systems, notices from other states about Taiwan-flagged vessels are treated as accepting Taiwan's inspection role and its exclusive authority. Both writers studied Taiwan's practice in detail, and China, which claims Taiwan, takes a different view of its status. So the flag works without any general rule saying that it must. It works because a real government supervises real ships and other states find it useful to deal with that government. The case does not help a private founder, since the acceptance depends on the supervision and on the size of the fleet. It does show that recognition of a flag can in practice come in pieces, body by body and subject by subject, and that the law of the sea has made room for that without settling the larger question.
cases.mechanism: A government most states do not recognise keeps a working flag through practical arrangements with fishing bodies and other states.

Chen, Fishing entity enforcement in high seas fisheries, University of Southampton thesis, 2014
Hsiao, The International Legal Status of Unrecognized Claimants to Statehood: Taiwan and the TRNC, Issues & Studies 47(1), 2011
UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

aka: Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry
cases.recognition: A national flag of a recognised state, administered by a private company
cases.cost: Registry revenue about $24 million a year
cases.name: Liberian ship registry and LISCR
cases.founder: President William Tubman and Edward Stettinius; LISCR from 1999
cases.story: Liberia's ship register began in 1948 under President William V.S. Tubman, with help from Edward Stettinius, the former US Secretary of State. The first commercial ship, the World Peace, was registered on 11 March 1949. An open register lets foreign owners fly a country's flag for a fee, and Liberia's grew quickly, to about 75 million gross tons by the mid-1970s. The register has always been run largely from the United States. The International Trust Company managed it until 1999. That year Charles Taylor's government appointed the Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry, or LISCR, to manage the register and collect the fees and taxes due to the state. LISCR is a limited liability company registered in Delaware and based in Virginia. Its appointment rests on an Act of the Liberian Legislature, and the statute limits its investors to US nationals. The money has been significant for a poor country. The register produces roughly $24 million a year. During the war, maritime funds made up about 70 percent of government revenue, and in the 1990s officials often squeezed the register for money to fund conflicts or for personal gain. In the 2007-08 budget the expected revenue of $13 million was about six percent of the total, and revenues now flow directly to the Ministry of Finance. As of December 2008 the flag covered more than 2,978 vessels. The case matters because it shows a sovereign power being operated as a contract. A private company in another country carries out the daily work of a national flag. The flag is still Liberia's, and only Liberia's law can create it or end the arrangement. A founder could use the service like any shipowner, and doing so would give a ship Liberian nationality and Liberian duties and nothing beyond those.
cases.mechanism: A state can contract out the running of its flag to a foreign company. Nationality still comes from the state, which can change the contract by law.

International Registries, Wikipedia

cases.recognition: A national flag of a recognised state, supported by a private company
cases.name: International Registries and the Marshall Islands flag
cases.founder: Government of the Marshall Islands, with International Registries, Inc.
cases.story: International Registries, Inc., known as IRI, is a company in Reston, Virginia, that runs the ship and corporate registries of the Republic of the Marshall Islands, a small Pacific country. The company began as Stettinius Associates-Liberia, founded in 1948 by Edward Stettinius to run Liberia's flag of convenience. A flag of convenience is a register open to foreign owners, usually for lower cost or lighter rules. After a series of mergers the firm became IRI. One account says it moved its registry from Liberia to the Marshall Islands after Liberia's president, Charles Taylor, demanded too much money. The Marshall Islands' registry program dates from 1988, when its government began it. A presentation given through the International Maritime Organization describes how the work is divided. IRI provides administrative and technical support for the maritime and corporate registries. That covers registering and administering vessels, safety inspections, seafarer identification, radio licences, ship security and investigations. Before a ship is accepted, its age, condition and certificates are checked, its owner and operator are vetted, and its record of port inspections is reviewed. Vessels, seafarers, companies and beneficial owners are screened against sanctions lists. The law it applies is the Marshall Islands Maritime Act and its regulations. This shows two things for anyone hoping to deal with such a flag. A company headquartered in the United States carries out the checks, so a founder's application goes through sanctions screening and other commercial vetting before any government officer is involved. The flag also has some standing in legal writing. The writer Eduardo Cavalcanti de Mello Filho gives the Marshall Islands as an example of a small state that can be a responsible flag. A founder seeking a flag with no supervision would be going to the wrong place, and a founder seeking a respectable one would receive that country's law on board.
cases.mechanism: A small country's flag is administered by a US company that vets ships and owners, so the private operator acts as an early gate.

cases.recognition: Joint submission endorsed at the UN in April 2011, according to the Commonwealth Secretariat
cases.name: Mauritius-Seychelles Joint Management Area
cases.story: The Mascarene Plateau is a long underwater ridge in the western Indian Ocean. It holds several shallow banks, including Saya de Malha, which founders have looked at since the 1990s as a site for new countries. Under the law of the sea a coastal state's seabed rights can extend beyond 200 nautical miles if the geology qualifies, while the water above remains high seas. Mauritius and Seychelles did not divide this area between them. They filed a joint submission for an extended continental shelf, and on 12 March 2012, during Mauritius's National Day celebrations, they signed a treaty to manage it together. The Commonwealth Secretariat described it as the world's largest offshore joint management area, covering 400,000 square kilometres of seabed, and said the UN had endorsed the submission in April 2011. The treaty provides for managing seabed resources for mutual benefit, offshore exploration and development, conservation of marine species and protection of the marine environment. Seychelles later prepared a Mascarene Plateau Bill in 2023, and a joint commission oversees the area. Public documents do not agree fully on how this applies to Saya de Malha. A note from a 2022 scientific expedition says the claim was made to include the bank, that the seabed is under joint management, and that the water remains high seas, with unclear responsibility for seabed creatures such as sea cucumbers. A paper from the southern Indian Ocean fisheries body refers to Mauritius's claim of historical rights over the bank, and asks whether that letter is the legal evaluation Mauritius had promised. For a founder the result is that a site once described as beyond every country's reach now has two governments with a treaty over its floor. Anything built on or fixed to that seabed would be measured against Articles 60 and 80 of UNCLOS, while ships in the water above keep their high-seas rights.
cases.mechanism: Two states jointly claim the seabed under a shallow plateau, leaving the water above as high seas and reducing what a founder can do on the bottom.

cases.recognition: Commission review on hold; no agreement among the four states
cases.name: Hatton-Rockall overlapping shelf claims
cases.founder: Ireland, the United Kingdom, Iceland and Denmark for the Faroe Islands
cases.story: The Hatton-Rockall area is a stretch of shallow seabed in the North Atlantic, west of Ireland and Scotland. Rockall itself is a tiny rock that has drawn founders and protesters, including Tom McClean in 1985 and Greenpeace's Global State of Waveland in 1997. The seabed around it matters for a different reason, because four states claim it as continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles. An Irish minister set out the position in a written answer to parliament in June 2019. Ireland and the United Kingdom agreed on the boundary between their shares in 1988. Iceland and Denmark, acting for the Faroe Islands, do not accept their claims beyond 200 nautical miles and have made their own. Ireland and the United Kingdom filed submissions with the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf in March 2009, which met Ireland's May 2009 deadline. Denmark filed in 2010. Iceland has not filed. The Commission does not review submissions covering disputed areas without the consent of all states concerned. Iceland does not consent, so the submissions are on hold. The four countries have met regularly since 2001 to try to resolve the overlap and have not reached agreement. This is a useful picture of an unresolved shelf. The water above beyond 200 miles stays high seas, as UNCLOS says. The floor is claimed four ways, and the expert process that could fix the limits cannot start. A founder might see an unfinished map. The treaty points the other way, since Article 77 says shelf rights do not depend on occupation or proclamation, so the seabed is treated as belonging to whichever state's claim proves good. A newcomer on the bottom would therefore have four governments with reason to object.
cases.mechanism: Where four states claim the same shelf and the UN process is blocked, the seabed remains contested among them, which gives a newcomer no place in the dispute.

cases.stopped_by: Malaysian government, which revoked the resort's licence on 6 January 2025
cases.challenge: Also claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam
cases.recognition: Held by Malaysia; other claimants dispute it
cases.name: Layang-Layang (Swallow Reef) base and dive resort
cases.founder: Royal Malaysian Navy; resort under Malaysian licence
cases.story: Layang-Layang, also called Swallow Reef, is an atoll in the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea. It shows what a commercial business looks like on a disputed reef under the protection of one claimant state. Malaysia's PASKAL special forces put up a plaque on the reef on 21 June 1980. In May 1983 eighteen of them built the first encampment, and the Royal Malaysian Navy has kept a station there since. Land reclamation raised the area from 6.2 hectares to 35 hectares, and a 2003 airport expansion extended the island to more than 1.5 kilometres. The airport has a concrete runway 1,367 metres long, two hangars, a radar station and a control tower. Personnel rotate on three-month deployments from Kota Kinabalu, and assault craft and guns are placed around the reef. China, Taiwan and Vietnam all claim it as well. A three-star dive resort operated on the island, and that gave the reef a civilian, commercial use under Malaysian licence. On 6 January 2025 Malaysia revoked the resort's operating licence, and it closed. The navy station remained. Its original land area was small, and whether the natural reef would count as an island or a low-tide elevation is a separate question. Reclamation would not change the answer under the reasoning of the 2016 South China Sea award, which judged features by their natural state. For anyone thinking of a partnership with a claimant, the lessons are plain. The business could operate because a navy was next door. It had no rights against that navy's government, and its closure came from the partner itself, with no rival state having to act.
cases.mechanism: A commercial operator on a disputed reef relies wholly on one claimant's licence, and that claimant can withdraw it at any time.

sources.t: Layang-Layang Island, Wikipedia
South China Sea Arbitration tribunal press release, 12 July 2016

cases.name: Attempts to buy Sealand
cases.founder: The Pirate Bay; InmoNaranja as selling agent
cases.story: Sealand has been offered for sale more than once, and each episode shows what buying it could and could not bring. Sealand is a Second World War sea fort on two concrete legs, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk, which the Bates family has called an independent principality since 1967. The first episode went badly for the family. In 1978 Alexander Achenbach, a German who described himself as Sealand's prime minister, invited Roy and Joan Bates to Austria to discuss a sale. While they were away his hired men took over the fort. The Bates family retook it by helicopter and held Achenbach's lawyer for about six weeks. In January 2007 The Pirate Bay, a website that indexes file-sharing links, tried to buy Sealand after harsher copyright measures in Sweden pushed it to look for a base elsewhere. Between 2007 and 2010 Sealand was offered for sale through a Spanish estate company, InmoNaranja, at an asking price of €750 million, then about £600 million. No sale was completed. The legal background made any sale an unusual one. Since 1 October 1987 the fort has stood inside Britain's 12-mile territorial sea. A court in Cologne held in 1978 that Sealand has no real territory, population or effective government, and no state recognises it. A buyer could at most have received possession of the structure and the family's claims. Whatever Britain's tolerance is worth, it was a decision about one family doing little harm, and a site for file-sharing would have asked Britain to think again. HavenCo's experience on the same fort between 2000 and 2008 suggests the same limit, since a data-hosting firm that relied on the location for protection from courts could not keep customers or the site. Roy Bates died in 2012 and his son Michael took over, and the family continues to sell titles rather than the fort.
cases.mechanism: A sale of a micronation can pass the structure and the story. It cannot pass recognition or the coastal state's tolerance.

sources.t: Principality of Sealand, Wikipedia
Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
HavenCo, Wikipedia

cases.stopped_by: Fatal implosion during a dive to the Titanic wreck, June 2023
cases.challenge: Investigations by Canadian and US authorities; no flag state existed
cases.name: Titan, the unregistered OceanGate submersible
cases.story: Titan was a small submersible built and run by the American company OceanGate to carry paying passengers to the wreck of the Titanic, 372 nautical miles south-southeast of Cape Race in Newfoundland. It imploded on a dive in June 2023. It claimed no independence, and it matters here as the clearest modern example of a crewed vessel working in open ocean with no flag. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada set out the position in its report M23A0169. "The Titan and the LARS were not registered in any country", the report says, the LARS being the launch and recovery system. They were not certified by any maritime authority or classification society. OceanGate had begun registering the first version of the craft in the Bahamas in August 2019, and it did not pursue that after learning the requirements. The Bahamas requires crewed submersibles to be registered, classed and in line with its rules. The dive site lay beyond Canada's 200-nautical-mile zone. The report notes that Canadian registration rules cover Canadian vessels everywhere and vessels in Canadian waters or its zone, and that Canada has no comprehensive rules for building or operating crewed submersibles. International guidance, the International Maritime Organization's Circular 981, is not binding. The support ship, Polar Prince, was Canadian-flagged and classed. So a regulated ship launched an unregulated craft from a place where no coastal state had authority. The report says UNCLOS requires ships to be registered in a single state. The board recommended that Canada set criteria for overseeing commercial vessels not registered or captured by port inspections, press the International Maritime Organization to make the guidance binding, and require submersibles operating with a Canadian support ship to comply. These are aimed at the support ship, because that is where a state can reach. The case shows that having no flag can last for years in practice, and that no one aboard gained any protection from it.
cases.mechanism: A crewed submersible operated in open ocean with no flag or certification. It was reached through its support ship and its company only after it was lost.

sources.t: Transportation Safety Board of Canada, marine investigation report M23A0169

cases.recognition: UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf ruled for Russia in March 2014
cases.name: Peanut Hole, Sea of Okhotsk
cases.founder: Russia, through its submission to the UN shelf commission
cases.story: The Peanut Hole is a strip of international water in the middle of the Sea of Okhotsk, about 55 kilometres wide and 480 kilometres long. It lies more than 200 nautical miles from any coast, so it falls outside the exclusive economic zone of Russia, which surrounds it. That makes it high seas, open to ships of all countries, in the middle of a sea otherwise under one country's resource control. Its name became known through fishing. Because any country could fish there, many did in 1991, and by 1992 they had taken perhaps as much as one million metric tons of pollock. Russia saw this as a threat, since the fish move between the pocket and its zone. In 1993 China, Japan, Poland, Russia and South Korea agreed to stop fishing there until stocks recovered, although they did not agree on what would follow. The seabed then took a different path from the water. Russia argued to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf that the sea floor there is part of its continental shelf. A subcommittee accepted this in November 2013, and in March 2014 the full commission agreed. Since then the seabed and subsoil have been treated as part of Russia's shelf, while the water remains high seas. This shows how the law of the sea can split a place in two. A ship may sail there under its own flag as on any open ocean. Anything fixed to the bottom meets Article 80 of UNCLOS, which gives the coastal state control over artificial islands and certain structures on its shelf. A founder who saw an empty pocket of high seas on a map would find, on looking closer, that the ground under it has an owner, and that the same owner surrounds it on all sides.
cases.mechanism: A pocket of high seas is ringed by one state's zone, and that state later secured the seabed underneath, so only the water stays open.

cases.recognition: Adopted by consensus of all 193 members on 24 September 2026
cases.name: UN declaration on sea-level rise and statehood
cases.founder: UN General Assembly; pressed by the Pacific Islands Forum and small island states
cases.story: On 24 September 2026 the UN General Assembly adopted a political declaration on sea-level rise by consensus of all 193 member states. It affirms a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, along with sovereignty, sovereign rights and responsibilities, and UN membership. It also says that once baselines have been established under the Law of the Sea treaty, states may keep their maritime zones despite physical changes from rising seas. The path to it ran through small island states. The Pacific Islands Forum issued declarations on maritime zones in 2021 and on statehood in 2023, arguing that a state continues to exist even if its territory is fully inundated. The International Law Commission backed that view in 2025, and the General Assembly recognised its contribution without endorsing its conclusions. A 2025 General Assembly resolution affirming continuity passed with eight states against and 28 abstaining, according to the account by Harry Aitken, an Australian legal adviser writing in a personal capacity. In its 2025 climate opinion the International Court of Justice said losing territory "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Judges Tomka and Aurescu criticised its ambiguity, and Tomka wrote that "territory has been indispensable to the concept of a State". The declaration does not explain how the principles would work in practice. It speaks of relocation as something that may be needed, that must be voluntary and consistent with international law, and that it calls "mobility with dignity". The only concrete step Aitken cites is the 2024 treaty between Australia and Tuvalu. For anyone interested in places outside existing countries, the point is that the requirement of territory has been loosened only for existing states. Nothing in the declaration helps a new body with no territory become a state. It also says nothing about artificial structures. Whether it becomes binding law will depend on how states act.
cases.mechanism: States agreed by consensus to presume that a state survives losing its land. The presumption protects existing states and creates no route for new ones.

sources.t: Aitken, Landmark UN Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, Just Security, 6 Oct 2026
